item.title: Nigerian Artists Who Have Sold Out London’s O2 Arena
item.description: The O2 Arena is one of the most popular music venues in the world. Its significance extends to Nigerian music. As Afrobeats was crossing over to the world, selling out London’s 02 Arena became one of the markers of that global expansion. Ayo Onikoyi , for Vanguard Newspaper , described the venue as “a symbol of global acceptance, a stamp of credibility, and a gateway to even greater success” for Nigerian artists. Filling a room with 1000 people requires a lot of work; now multiply that by 20, and imagine what how much effort it’d take to fill out a venue with 20, 000 people, screaming back your music at you. The London’s 02 Arena has a 20,000-seat capacity, and has become one of the most recognisable stages in Afrobeats’ international rise, offering artists an opportunity to perform before large audiences, connect with Nigerians and other African music lovers in the diaspora, and demonstrate the growing commercial appeal of Nigerian music. Its reputation as a venue for global superstars has also made performing there a significant career milestone. If you can sell out the 02 Arena, you could dare to sell out a bigger venue, stadiums, and many more, in the world. Being very popular in Nigeria does not translate to selling out venues like the O2 Arena; your music must have travelled far. Wizkid opened the 022 Arena door when he sold out the O2 Arena in 2018, becoming the first Nigerian artist to achieve the feat. Since then, Davido , Burna Boy , Asake and Rema have also taken their music to the celebrated London venue, with some returning for multiple shows. Here are the Nigerian artists who have sold out the O2 Arena: Wizkid Wizkid made history on 26 May 2018 when he sold out the O2 Arena with his Afrorepublik concert, becoming the first Nigerian artist to achieve the feat. The show featured appearances by other Nigerian and UK-based artists, including Tiwa Savage, Mr Eazi and many others. It marked a major moment for Afrobeats, demonstrating that Nigerian music could command a 20,000-capacity venue in London. He returned in 2021 during the Made in Lagos tour, when he sold out the iconic venues within minutes, and performed for three consecutive days. Davido On 27 January 2019, Davido headlined a sold-out show at the O2 Arena. The concert featured special appearances, including British actor Idris Elba and Jamaican artist Popcaan , and showcased Davido’s ability to bring his energetic performances and catalogue of hits to an international audience. item.dc:creator: BellaNaija Features
item.content:encoded: The O2 Arena is one of the most popular music venues in the world. Its significance extends to Nigerian music. As Afrobeats was crossing over to the world, selling out London’s 02 Arena became one of the markers of that global expansion. Ayo Onikoyi , for Vanguard Newspaper , described the venue as “a symbol of global acceptance, a stamp of credibility, and a gateway to even greater success” for Nigerian artists. Filling a room with 1000 people requires a lot of work; now multiply that by 20, and imagine what how much effort it’d take to fill out a venue with 20, 000 people, screaming back your music at you. The London’s 02 Arena has a 20,000-seat capacity, and has become one of the most recognisable stages in Afrobeats’ international rise, offering artists an opportunity to perform before large audiences, connect with Nigerians and other African music lovers in the diaspora, and demonstrate the growing commercial appeal of Nigerian music. Its reputation as a venue for global superstars has also made performing there a significant career milestone. If you can sell out the 02 Arena, you could dare to sell out a bigger venue, stadiums, and many more, in the world. Being very popular in Nigeria does not translate to selling out venues like the O2 Arena; your music must have travelled far. Wizkid opened the 022 Arena door when he sold out the O2 Arena in 2018, becoming the first Nigerian artist to achieve the feat. Since then, Davido , Burna Boy , Asake and Rema have also taken their music to the celebrated London venue, with some returning for multiple shows. Here are the Nigerian artists who have sold out the O2 Arena: Wizkid Wizkid made history on 26 May 2018 when he sold out the O2 Arena with his Afrorepublik concert, becoming the first Nigerian artist to achieve the feat. The show featured appearances by other Nigerian and UK-based artists, including Tiwa Savage, Mr Eazi and many others. It marked a major moment for Afrobeats, demonstrating that Nigerian music could command a 20,000-capacity venue in London. He returned in 2021 during the Made in Lagos tour, when he sold out the iconic venues within minutes, and performed for three consecutive days. Davido On 27 January 2019, Davido headlined a sold-out show at the O2 Arena. The concert featured special appearances, including British actor Idris Elba and Jamaican artist Popcaan , and showcased Davido’s ability to bring his energetic performances and catalogue of hits to an international audience. The milestone further strengthened his position as one of Afrobeats’ leading global stars. Burna Boy Burna Boy sold out the O2 Arena on 27 August 2021 during his Spaceship tour. Asake After rising rapidly through the Nigerian music scene with hits, Asake took another major step in his career when he sold out the O2 Arena on 20 August 2023. The show followed his successful sold-out performances at the smaller O2 Academy Brixton venue. He returned to the O2 Arena in 2024 for his Lungu Boy World Tour, reinforcing his growing international appeal and the reach of his distinctive street-pop sound, and returned again in 2026 during his In God We Trust tour. Rema Rema joined the list on 14 November 2023 when he sold out the O2 Arena. At just 23, he became one of the youngest Nigerian artists to headline a sold-out concert at the venue. The show featured an elaborate entrance, a live band and performances of songs from his growing catalogue, including his global hit “Calm Down.” It was a defining moment for the singer. Now, Olamide has announced his upcoming show at the O2 Arena in March 2027. The O2 Arena remains one of the most significant stages for Nigerian artists seeking to cement their place on the global music scene, and Olamide’s planned performance will be another important moment for Afrobeats. It will add his name to the growing list of Nigerian artists who have taken their music to the celebrated London venue, further demonstrating how far Nigerian music has travelled and how much further it can go. item.title: Admin: 'I spent all weekend on my servers' after Microsoft breaks Exchange Server with October updates
item.description: Microsoft has acknowledged that the October 2026 Windows Server updates may be destabilizing Exchange Server. The problems are related to this list of Windows Server updates (see here ) and Microsoft makes it clear they are not related to the October 2026 security updates for Exchange Server. The software giant says the bug can hit Exchange Servers running Windows Server 2016, 2019, 2022, and 2025. The glitch might not be immediate and could impact Exchange Server OWA, which can throw up connection glitches or cause lengthy email queues, "with email crawling to a halt." Rebooting the server might make the problem go away temporarily, but a more permanent workaround is a registry edit. The destabilization issue could impact Exchange Server 2016, 2019, and the new Subscription Edition (SE), says the Windows maker. Microsoft strongly advised that customers should not uninstall the October 2026 Windows Server update and stated, "Not all Exchange servers will be impacted by installation of those updates equally; the severity and speed of impact varies based on Exchange server load. Some servers might never see a problem." However, for those administrators who found their weekend swallowed by borked Exchange Servers, the registry edit is currently the only workaround. The cause of the issue is a default limit on the amount of memory used by Endpoint Mapper when handling Endpoint Lookup calls. In Microsoft's Release Health Dashboard for Windows Server 2025 (Server 2022, 2019, and 2016 are also affected), the Microsoft said: "For workloads such as Exchange Server, the default limit of 512 simultaneous Endpoint Lookup calls might not be sufficient under heavy load." Hence, the instruction to use a registry setting to increase the maximum. It added, "We are investigating this issue and will provide more information when it is available." Customers were understandably frustrated. On Microsoft's support page, one wrote, "We have had the problem like every 20h since Wednesday, when we installed the windows updates for October and the exchange su. Reboot only solution," before noting that the registry setting appeared to have improved things. Another fumed , "Also please release your updates tested and without problems. Without giving us the job to test for you. We're already paying for the software and you want to make tests with us?! I spent all weekend on my servers because of this." The issue is bad form on the part of Microsoft and appears to be the result of a poorly thought-through default applied in the operating system which impacted Exchange Server. Microsoft has yet to commit to issuing an out-of-band update to resolve the issue, after all, not every customer is affected, and the problem depends heavily on how busy a server is. However, at least there's a registry workaround that might do the trick while Microsoft ponders its next move. ®

item.title: From a Casual Night Out to a Brand-New Car: How Queen Thompson Won Big in the Guinness ‘Open For More’ Promo!
item.description: When you head out for a night of good vibes with your friends, you expect great conversations, plenty of laughter, and maybe a few photos for the Gram. What you probably don’t expect is to walk away with the chance to win a brand-new car! That was the unexpected turn Queen Thompson ’s evening took when she became the grand prize winner of the recently concluded 10-week Guinness ‘Open For More’ promo. It started as a regular night out in Akwa Ibom. Queen and her friends had gone to one of their favourite spots to unwind, catch up and enjoy some chilled drinks. Among the bottles on the table was Guinness Foreign Extra Stout . At some point during the evening, Queen noticed the promo code beneath her bottle cap, brought out her phone, and entered it. Nothing elaborate, just a quick entry while enjoying the night. Little did she know that one simple entry would put her in the running for a brand-new Toyota Land Cruiser Prado worth ₦150 million! A few weeks later, Queen received a phone call from an official Guinness representative with news that would have anyone asking, “ Wait, what?! Is this for real? ” She had won the grand prize! But excitement wasn’t her first reaction. Having been defrauded twice earlier in the year, Queen was understandably cautious and initially wondered if the call was another scam. It took the official prize presentation for the news to fully sink in. At the handover ceremony at Guinness Nigeria’s headquarters in Ogba, Lagos, Queen’s win became official in the most memorable way. Girish Sharma , Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of Guinness Nigeria Plc , personally presented her with the keys to her brand-new Toyota Land Cruiser Prado, as company executives, brand representatives, fellow prize winners and well-wishers gathered to celebrate the moment. Still taking it all in, Queen said, “I am still in shock! I never imagined that opening a bottle of Guinness Foreign Extra Stout would lead to me driving home in a brand-new Toyota Land Cruiser Prado. When I got the notification, I initially doubted it because I had been defrauded twice earlier this year. I am so grateful to Guinness for this incredible, life-changing gift. Truly, what God cannot do does not exist!” Now that’s one night out that ended with a plot twist nobody saw coming! The Guinness ‘Open For More’ promo may have wrapped up, but the winners’ stories remain memorable, especially the grand winner whose experience leaves us with a little reminder: stay open to possibilities; you never know when good news might be on the other end of a call. Queen’s story was the grand finale of a much bigger journey. Over 10 weeks, Guinness Nigeria rewarded 1,075 consumers across the country, with 1,000 people winning ₦100,000 each and another 75 becoming millionaires with ₦1 million apiece, before Queen drove home with the grand prize, a Toyota Land Cruiser Prado valued at ₦150 million. For Guinness, Open For More was a way to give something back to the consumers wh

item.title: Before They Say “I Do”, See Zlatan Ibile & Davita Omoniyi’s Pre-Wedding Photos
item.description: Zlatan Ibile and Davita Omoniyi in an intimate pre-wedding portrait. Can you hear the wedding bells? Something beautiful is happening in Zlatan Ibile ’s world, and this time, it has nothing to do with a new song or music video. The Afrobeats star, whose real name is Omoniyi Temidayo Raphael , is getting ready to celebrate his love for longtime partner Davita Omoniyi in a grand wedding ceremony on 24 October 2026. And while we’re still waiting to see what the couple have planned for their big day, their pre-wedding photographs are already giving us plenty to admire. From the gorgeous colour choices to the fashion and the sweet way they pose together, Zlatan and Davita are making the countdown to their wedding even more exciting. The couple have been together for years and share two children. Davita, a UK-based media personality and entrepreneur, reportedly took on the Omoniyi surname following their private civil registry ceremony earlier this year. Now, with their wedding celebration approaching, they’re preparing to mark another chapter of their relationship surrounded by family and friends. Zlatan Ibile and Davita Omoniyi posing together in pastel outfits for their official pre-wedding pictures. For their pre-wedding photographs, celebrity stylist Emmanuel Goodnews Icon brought together a lovely combination of pastel ice blue and blush pink against a rich teal studio backdrop. The colours worked beautifully together, with Davita’s gown and Zlatan’s tailored outfit offering two different takes on the same colour palette. Davita wore a strapless mermaid gown by Lasosa By Pam Pam, featuring micro-pleating and ruching across the bodice. The fitted silhouette opened into a voluminous bubble-hem train made from bubblegum pink taffeta, giving the dress an interesting contrast of structure and volume. She completed her look with a high braided ponytail, glowing makeup, a classic tennis necklace and matching diamond jewellery. Davita Omoniyi in a custom gown by Lasosa By Pam Pam styled by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon. Beside her, Zlatan wore a bespoke light blue two-piece suit by T.I Nathan. His jacket featured a structured mandarin collar and concealed button placket, paired with relaxed wide-leg trousers. Dark wire-frame glasses and black patent leather shoes completed his look, keeping the styling simple while allowing the tailoring and colour to take centre stage. Zlatan Ibile styled by Emmanuel Goodnews Icon in a bespoke T.I Nathan suit The rich teal backdrop made the soft colours of their outfits even more striking, while their poses brought a lovely sense of closeness to the portraits. With 24 October just around the corner, the couple have given us a beautiful first look at their wedding style, and we’re curious to see what they’ll wear when the celebrations begin. item.title: Microsoft abandons UK AI supercomputer as grid struggles to keep up
item.description: Microsoft has reportedly pulled out of plans for Britain's largest AI supercomputer, because the government-backed project is facing the rather inconvenient problem of having no electricity to run it. The tech giant has terminated its agreement with British AI infrastructure startup Nscale for a planned datacenter in Loughton, Essex, according to The Telegraph, which first reported the withdrawal on Sunday. The decision follows reports that the site, which was supposed to begin operating in 2027, might not receive enough electricity from the grid until the early to mid-2030s. Microsoft was expected to be the anchor customer at Loughton, which Nscale had pitched as the UK's largest sovereign AI datacenter. Its departure leaves Nscale without a publicly announced customer for the site, although the neocloud insists the project is still going ahead. When the deal was announced in September 2025, the plan was to pack 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs into a 50MW facility, with room to expand to 90MW. Microsoft would use the computing power for its Azure cloud services, with the first chips expected in early 2027. One important detail remained: how to power it. As The Guardian reported last month , UK Power Networks warned Nscale that the grid capacity needed might not be available until the 2030s. A UK Power Networks spokesperson told The Register it could not discuss individual connections due to obligations under Section 105 of the Utilities Act. "However, in general, many datacenters, whilst they can connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the national transmission network which we do not own," the spokesperson said. Nscale, meanwhile, isn't letting the small matter of losing its biggest customer dampen its enthusiasm. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK. Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts,” Nscale told The Register . Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment. The project has already had its share of awkward moments. In March, it was revealed that the site earmarked for Britain's AI supercomputer was still being used as a scaffolding yard. Nscale has since cleared the land, but removing the scaffolding has proved easier than securing electricity. The government might be feeling a little red-faced too, having trumpeted the Loughton project as part of Microsoft's £22 billion UK investment announcement in September 2025 . Just over a year later, Microsoft has walked away, and the site is still facing years of delays in getting the power it needs. The grid problems extend well beyond Essex. Its departure leaves Nscale without a publicly announced customer for the site, although the neocloud insists the project is still going ahead. When the deal was announced in September 2025, the plan was to pack 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs into a 50MW facility, with room to expand to 90MW. Microsoft would use the computing power for its Azure cloud services, with the first chips expected in early 2027. One important detail remained: how to power it. As The Guardian reported last month , UK Power Networks warned Nscale that the grid capacity needed might not be available until the 2030s. A UK Power Networks spokesperson told The Register it could not discuss individual connections due to obligations under Section 105 of the Utilities Act. "However, in general, many datacenters, whilst they can connect to our distribution network, are awaiting works on the national transmission network which we do not own," the spokesperson said. Nscale, meanwhile, isn't letting the small matter of losing its biggest customer dampen its enthusiasm. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK. Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts,” Nscale told The Register . Microsoft did not respond to a request for comment. The project has already had its share of awkward moments. In March, it was revealed that the site earmarked for Britain's AI supercomputer was still being used as a scaffolding yard. Nscale has since cleared the land, but removing the scaffolding has proved easier than securing electricity. The government might be feeling a little red-faced too, having trumpeted the Loughton project as part of Microsoft's £22 billion UK investment announcement in September 2025 . Just over a year later, Microsoft has walked away, and the site is still facing years of delays in getting the power it needs. The grid problems extend well beyond Essex. Ofgem proposed charging datacenter developers for connection requests earlier this year, hoping to discourage speculative projects from clogging up the queue. Demand for new connections had surged from 41GW to 125GW in less than a year, with datacenters accounting for at least 80GW. Some UK datacenter developers have turned to gas-powered generation rather than wait years for a grid connection, while others face growing resistance from the people living nearby. Residents near Google's Waltham Cross facility complained about noise, lighting and poor consultation at a public meeting in July. Britain isn’t alone in finding that the AI boom comes with substantial infrastructure demands. In the US, public enthusiasm for datacenters appears to be cooling, with concerns about electricity costs and environmental impacts increasingly souring attitudes towards new developments. For all the billions being thrown at AI infrastructure, the industry is discovering that building datacenters is the easy part. Getting them connected to the grid, and keeping the neighbors happy, is proving rather more difficult. ®

item.title: Did a giant object collide with Earth to form the moon?
item.description:
Micah Hanks is a science reporter and podcaster focusing on space and astronomy, and Editor at TheDebrief.org. Follow him on X @MicahHanks.

For as long as humans have watched the night sky, we have wondered about the moon , pondering everything from its alien appearance to its influence over phenomena on Earth such as ocean tides, climate stability, and even the natural rhythms of many organisms. Among the many questions we have about Earth's lone natural satellite, one remains preeminent: what are the moon's origins , and how long has it orbited Earth? Today, the leading theory among astronomers is that deep in our planet's past — perhaps within roughly the first 100 million years of solar system history — Earth collided with a planet-sized object, creating the moon within a period that may have been as short as just a few hours . Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia. The material ejected into orbit by the powerful impact in question would have accumulated afterward, forming the moon that we observe today. What do we know? Birth of a lunar origin hypothesis The evolution of this striking solution to one of the moon's most enduring mysteries goes back to 1946, when geologist Reginald Aldworth Daly was among the first to suggest that an impact event might explain the formation of the moon. Before Daly, scientists had been leaning toward theories that involved Earth's rapid spin billions of years ago, when each day may have at one time lasted as little as 2 or 3 hours . Decades later in the 1970s, researchers William Hartmann and Donald Davis developed their own models involving collisions of large bodies left over from planetary formation, which could collide with younger planets. Building on such ideas, other researchers went on to propose similar scenarios between the early Earth and a Mars-sized object. Early in the following decade, the concept eventually claimed its place as the leading lunar-formation process during a landmark conference held in Kona, Hawaii, in 1984. Earth's moon is thought to have formed when a Mars-sized object, called Theia, slammed into the proto-Earth more than 4.4 billion years ago, blasting out material that later coalesced into a large satellite as depicted in this artist's illustration. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Evidence of a planetary-scale collision The popularity of the giant-impact hypothesis can be attributed to the multiple lines of evidence supporting the impact scenario. For instance, researchers have long recognized the similar stable-isotope ratios between both moon rocks and those from Earth, strongly suggesting a link between their origins. Additionally, the unusually high angular momentum (or spin) of the Earth-moon system, when compared to observations of other rocky planets, also cou

Known as the giant-impact hypothesis, this proposed event involves a hypothetical Mars-sized protoplanet astronomers call Theia. The material ejected into orbit by the powerful impact in question would have accumulated afterward, forming the moon that we observe today. What do we know? Birth of a lunar origin hypothesis The evolution of this striking solution to one of the moon's most enduring mysteries goes back to 1946, when geologist Reginald Aldworth Daly was among the first to suggest that an impact event might explain the formation of the moon. Before Daly, scientists had been leaning toward theories that involved Earth's rapid spin billions of years ago, when each day may have at one time lasted as little as 2 or 3 hours . Decades later in the 1970s, researchers William Hartmann and Donald Davis developed their own models involving collisions of large bodies left over from planetary formation, which could collide with younger planets. Building on such ideas, other researchers went on to propose similar scenarios between the early Earth and a Mars-sized object. Early in the following decade, the concept eventually claimed its place as the leading lunar-formation process during a landmark conference held in Kona, Hawaii, in 1984. Earth's moon is thought to have formed when a Mars-sized object, called Theia, slammed into the proto-Earth more than 4.4 billion years ago, blasting out material that later coalesced into a large satellite as depicted in this artist's illustration. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech) Evidence of a planetary-scale collision The popularity of the giant-impact hypothesis can be attributed to the multiple lines of evidence supporting the impact scenario. For instance, researchers have long recognized the similar stable-isotope ratios between both moon rocks and those from Earth, strongly suggesting a link between their origins. Additionally, the unusually high angular momentum (or spin) of the Earth-moon system, when compared to observations of other rocky planets, also could be explained as one of the effects of a massive collision. Further clues can be found in the moon's composition, which reveals a relatively small iron core and lower density. This is significant to astronomers, since a hypothetical giant impact would have seen the suspected Theia protoplanet's metallic core merging with the young Earth's interior — meanwhile, lighter mantle and crust material from both worlds would have become dislodged and blasted into orbit, eventually helping form the moon. Another important piece of evidence involves the relative depletion of volatile substances (a chemical that easily turns into gas or vapor at room temperatures) in lunar material, which again suggests that it might have been lost during an extremely energetic event, an idea further supported by evidence that the early moon once possessed a substantial magma ocean. Illustration of the young Earth-Moon system. The Earth had recently formed when it was struck by a protoplanet, called Theia, roughly three times the size of Mars. Debris from the impact went into orbit where it quickly coalesced to form the Moon, probably within just a few thousand years. Initially the Earth and moon were much closer together than they are now, and spinning more quickly. In this depiction, debris from the collision continues to rain down on both worlds. (Image credit: Mark Garlick/Science Photo Library/Getty Images) What remains unknown? New research expands on the Theia hypothesis Still, several significant questions remain, including what precise conditions led to the impact, and how the resulting planetary material evolved into the moon as it appears today. Recently, a new study by Adeene Denton of Southwest Research Institute and colleagues at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory put a new spin on the Theia hypothesis, suggesting that the suspected ancient impact may have been significantly influenced by the heat and physical strength of the two colliding bodies. The team's findings challenge some long-held views about the giant-impact hypothesis, while lending new support to others. For instance, the team's simulations revealed that while some impacts lead to the creation of a disk of debris that later coalesces into a moon, under other conditions, simulations support the idea that the moon could have been formed in a remarkably short period of time — perhaps within around five hours . However, one of the primary issues with determining the exact conditions of the giant-impact hypothesis involves the ongoing debate over the moon's age. "There is a large controversy regarding the age of the moon," said Dr. Erik Asphaug, a planetary science professor at the University of Arizona's Lunar and Planetary Laboratory and one of the new study's co-authors. Earth sets over the moon's curved limb in this photo captured by the Artemis II crew during their journey around the far side of the moon. (Image credit: NASA) In an email to Space, Asphaug explained some of the issues arising from this, since current estimates place the timing of the moon's formation anywhere from around 40 to 120 million years after the formation of the solar system. Therein lies part of the issue, according to Asphaug, who says this timing could have significant implications for models of the Theia impact. If it had been an earlier collision, Asphaug says this would have involved a hotter Theia due to the greater degree of radiogenic heating; by contrast, a later impact would have meant a cooler and stronger Theia. "I don't think we know enough yet to say the moon (and by corollary, the Earth) formed this way or that way," Asphaug told Space . "But knowing how temperature affects the result opens up a new dimension for viewing the problem, and that is always helpful because it shifts our frame of reference, like getting out of the car to have a walk around." A lunar enigma in time and space For researchers like Asphaug, understanding the moon's formation requires looking at it as more than just an event in space, but also as one in time. Doing so allows comparisons between three different metrics: isotopic decay, temperature-dependent material strength, and the geological record of debris striking other planets — a process through which he believes tighter constraints could be placed on precisely when the moon-forming impact might have occurred. Adeene Denton, the study's lead author, also emphasized the introduction of the time component her team's research brings to the table, telling Space in an email that the outcome of the moon-forming impact could have depended significantly on the timing of the collision. "Before, scientists have generally assumed that the outcome of the collision will be the same regardless of when it takes place," Denton wrote . "But now we know that temperature's effect on material properties, which is dictated by how old and/or cold the proto-Earth and Theia might be, alters things substantially." B

item.title: An Icon Reimagined: Maltina Unveils New Look And Same Nourishing Taste
item.description: Maltina , Nigeria’s pioneering malt brand, has unveiled a new visual identity. The new look celebrates 50 years of nourishment while preserving the trusted taste Nigerians know and love. The new identity presents Maltina through a more contemporary lens across its glass bottles, cans and PET bottles. The brand’s signature orange has been strengthened, while enhanced gold elements create a more distinctive and premium presence on the shelf. New design cues, including the gold crown cork, brighter sunrays, a more prominent golden barley icon, a bolder calcium coin and the “Since 1976” heritage mark, bring Maltina’s story of nourishment and heritage to life. The look may be new, but the nourishing Maltina consumers know and trust remains unchanged. Maltina is fortified with calcium, with one 33cl bottle providing the equivalent of half a glass of milk. The brand is also endorsed by the Nutrition Society of Nigeria as a non-alcoholic drink rich in Vitamin A. “ For 50 years, Maltina has grown alongside generations of Nigerians. This refreshed identity is an evolution of a much-loved brand, designed to keep Maltina fresh, relevant and connected to today’s consumers while preserving the nourishing taste they know and trust, ” said Sarah Agha , Marketing Director, Nigerian Breweries Plc . Rather than define the new look for consumers, Maltina is inviting Nigerians to share their own first impressions through the “ What’s Your Word? ” campaign. Across media, retail and consumer experiences, people will be encouraged to look again and describe the refreshed identity in one word. “This relaunch is about more than a new pack. It is an invitation for Nigerians to help shape the next chapter of a brand that has been part of their lives for five decades. We look forward to hearing the words the new Maltina inspires,” Agha added. Consumers will encounter the refreshed packs in stores, restaurants, bars and markets, supported by a nationwide media rollout, trade launches and immersive consumer activations designed to help Nigerians discover and experience the new look. The invitation is simple: experience the new Maltina and tell us what you see. What’s Your Word for the New Maltina? https://maltina.nbplc.com/ . About Maltina Maltina is a non-alcoholic malt drink from Nigerian Breweries Plc. For 50 years, the brand has been part of Nigerian homes and everyday moments, bringing together nourishment, happiness and shared experiences across generations. item.title: Ayra Starr Is Taking Her Starrgirl World Tour to Europe and North America in 2027
item.description: Ayra Starr is set to bring her hit singles to the NFL London Game halftime show on 11th October Ladies and gentlemen, we reckon that cities in Europe, the UK and North America will come alive in purple from January 2027 to April 2027 because the Starrgirl herself, Ayra Starr , has officially announced her grand return to global stages. If you have been keeping up with global music headlines, you already know Oyinkansola Sarah Aderibigbe —famously known across the world as Ayra Starr—is in a league of her own. She recently made history as the very first African artiste to headline an NFL halftime show during the 2026 International Games fixture in London, treating a packed stadium crowd to a performance that cemented Afrobeats on one of sport’s biggest entertainment platforms. Fresh off that landmark milestone and the release of her third studio album, Starrgirl, the Mavin global sensation is packing her bags to take the project on a massive multi-continent run. Ayra Starr performing at the NFL Halftime Show in London The upcoming Starrgirl World Tour kicks off its main international leg on 20 January 2027 in Cologne, Germany. From there, Ayra heads to Amsterdam on 21 January, Paris on 24 January, Milan on 27 January, Zurich on 29 January, and Brussels on 31 January. Her UK lovers get their turn on 2 February 2027, when she steps onto the London stage for a night that promises to be an absolute highlight of the winter season. North American fans pick up the excitement starting 18 March 2027 in Houston, Texas. The road trip continues across Dallas, Atlanta, Silver Spring, Boston, Philadelphia, Brooklyn, Chicago, Minneapolis, Denver, and San Francisco, alongside Canadian stops in Toronto and Montreal through early April. If you have been looking for the perfect excuse to hear catalogue favourites alongside fresh hits off her latest project like “ Gimme Dat ,” “ Tornado ,” “ Hot Body ,” and “ Heaven Baby ” live in an arena full of fans singing every word, this is your sign to pack your bags, align your travel dates, and experience the Starrgirl World Tour firsthand. Ayra Starr returns with her third studio album, Starrgirl. The post Ayra Starr Is Taking Her Starrgirl World Tour to Europe and North America in 2027 appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Broadcom Wi-Fi bug turns sweet 16, still lets strangers hijack your router
item.description: A 16-year-old security flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi software could let attackers hijack millions of routers without knowing the network password, even though the chipmaker reportedly knew about the problem since 2018. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the vulnerability , dubbed "WPSplinter," revealing two bugs in Broadcom's proprietary Wi-Fi implementation that date back to at least 2010. An attempted fix arrived eight years later, but Kaiser claims it didn't fully resolve the problem. The bugs lie in Broadcom's handling of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets users connect devices to a wireless network without manually entering a password. Kaiser found that specially crafted WPS messages could corrupt the router's memory, allowing someone within Wi-Fi range to run their own code on the device. They wouldn't need the Wi-Fi password, and the router's owner wouldn't have to do a thing. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against routers supplied by Belgian internet providers Proximus and Orange. In one attack against an ASKEY TCG3000 gateway, he ran code on the device, pulled its Wi-Fi password from memory, and sent it back over the air. He then used the stolen credentials to join the network. He also found the flaw in Netgear and Technicolor routers supplied by VOO. He estimates that around 850,000 Proximus gateways could be affected, along with 500,000 at VOO and 210,000 at Orange Belgium. That puts the potential total at 1.56 million routers in Belgium alone, although Kaiser admits the figures are rough estimates. However, the problem is unlikely to stop at the Belgian border. Broadcom's Wi-Fi technology is used by dozens of manufacturers across hundreds of products, meaning the number of affected devices worldwide could be considerably higher. According to Kaiser, the chipmaker knew about the vulnerability back in 2018 and released a partial fix without publicly disclosing the problem. It subsequently recommended that manufacturers move away from its proprietary implementation and use the open-source hostapd software instead. Owners of routers running Broadcom's older eCos-based chips, including the BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, are in a particularly grim position. Kaiser calls the flaw a "forever day," meaning those devices may never get a fix. Routers using Linux-based BCM3390, BCM65xx, and BCM68xx chips aren't necessarily off the hook either, unless their manufacturers switch to hostapd. That leaves some older routers with no obvious route to a fix, while others depend on their manufacturers updating software that may be years out of support. Kaiser first reported the vulnerabilities to Broadcom on July 18, followed by a second report on July 27, giving the company and affected vendors 90 days before public disclosure. Broadcom responded on July 28 to say a patch was available and advised him to contact affected manufacturers directly. item.dc:creator: Carly Page
item.content:encoded: A 16-year-old security flaw in Broadcom's Wi-Fi software could let attackers hijack millions of routers without knowing the network password, even though the chipmaker reportedly knew about the problem since 2018. Security researcher Quentin Kaiser disclosed the vulnerability , dubbed "WPSplinter," revealing two bugs in Broadcom's proprietary Wi-Fi implementation that date back to at least 2010. An attempted fix arrived eight years later, but Kaiser claims it didn't fully resolve the problem. The bugs lie in Broadcom's handling of Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS), the feature that lets users connect devices to a wireless network without manually entering a password. Kaiser found that specially crafted WPS messages could corrupt the router's memory, allowing someone within Wi-Fi range to run their own code on the device. They wouldn't need the Wi-Fi password, and the router's owner wouldn't have to do a thing. Kaiser demonstrated working exploits against routers supplied by Belgian internet providers Proximus and Orange. In one attack against an ASKEY TCG3000 gateway, he ran code on the device, pulled its Wi-Fi password from memory, and sent it back over the air. He then used the stolen credentials to join the network. He also found the flaw in Netgear and Technicolor routers supplied by VOO. He estimates that around 850,000 Proximus gateways could be affected, along with 500,000 at VOO and 210,000 at Orange Belgium. That puts the potential total at 1.56 million routers in Belgium alone, although Kaiser admits the figures are rough estimates. However, the problem is unlikely to stop at the Belgian border. Broadcom's Wi-Fi technology is used by dozens of manufacturers across hundreds of products, meaning the number of affected devices worldwide could be considerably higher. According to Kaiser, the chipmaker knew about the vulnerability back in 2018 and released a partial fix without publicly disclosing the problem. It subsequently recommended that manufacturers move away from its proprietary implementation and use the open-source hostapd software instead. Owners of routers running Broadcom's older eCos-based chips, including the BCM3380, BCM3383, and BCM33834, are in a particularly grim position. Kaiser calls the flaw a "forever day," meaning those devices may never get a fix. Routers using Linux-based BCM3390, BCM65xx, and BCM68xx chips aren't necessarily off the hook either, unless their manufacturers switch to hostapd. That leaves some older routers with no obvious route to a fix, while others depend on their manufacturers updating software that may be years out of support. Kaiser first reported the vulnerabilities to Broadcom on July 18, followed by a second report on July 27, giving the company and affected vendors 90 days before public disclosure. Broadcom responded on July 28 to say a patch was available and advised him to contact affected manufacturers directly. The following day, however, the company declined to assign a CVE identifier or provide him with a copy of the notification it said it had sent to manufacturers through its customer portal. Kaiser also contacted Proximus, attempted to reach Orange Belgium and VOO, and passed his findings to Belgium's national cybersecurity authorities. He subsequently opened a case with CERT/CC, which closed it on August 4 because Broadcom was itself a CVE Numbering Authority and had declined to register the vulnerability. By October 15, a day before his presentation, Kaiser said none of the affected devices he had identified had received a patch. Kaiser hasn't reported evidence of attacks in the wild, but the potential for mischief is considerable. Someone parked outside a home or office could potentially compromise a vulnerable router, steal network credentials, or use their access to interfere with traffic. Kaiser also credited AI with speeding up the investigation. He reckons the work would ordinarily have taken him months, but with the help of frontier models, he finished it in less than a week. ®

item.title: Seven Women, Seven Innovations: InnovateNaija’s Role in Nigeria’s Tech Story
item.description: Through the NASENI and AfriLabs-backed InnovateNaija Challenge, seven women brought bold technological ideas to the national stage, and one of them took home the ultimate prize. Their journey shows what is possible when Nigerian women are given the platform, support, and opportunity to build. For years, conversations about Nigeria’s technology ecosystem have centred on the scale of the industry, the growth of startups, and the young people building the next generation of solutions. But there is another part of that story that deserves greater attention: the women building too. Seven women were among the 15 finalists of the InnovateNaija Challenge , a national technology and innovation competition led by the National Agency for Science and Engineering Infrastructure ( NASENI ), in partnership with AfriLabs and the Federal Ministry of Youth Development. Coming from different parts of the country and working across diverse fields, these women built solutions that go far beyond the idea of simply participating in technology. They designed, engineered, and developed products responding to real problems in healthcare, agriculture, energy, environmental sustainability, and everyday life. A Historic Victory for Agricultural Hardware The national pitch event, held October 6, 2026 , saw all 15 finalists present physical prototypes before industry experts, global investors, and policymakers. Emerging as the overall grand prize winner of ₦100 million was Abia State innovator Adaeze Ruth Akpagbula , co-founder of Farm Speak , for her PenKeep Smart Poultry Climate Control System . Designed to help farmers manage climate-related challenges across poultry, aquaculture, greenhouse, and smart irrigation systems, PenKeep demonstrates how deep tech can be applied to fundamental agricultural challenges. For Akpagbula, who identified funding, infrastructure, and electricity as major hurdles for hardware innovators in Nigeria, the ₦100 million award will help expand her company’s production capacity and enable the technology to reach more farmers. Innovating Across Every Sector Akpagbula’s top finish was part of a larger showing by female innovators across the competition. Among the seven female finalists was Kemisola Bolarinwa from Ekiti State, whose innovation, the Smart Bra Cup Diagnostic Device , explores the use of technology in breast health. Her work demonstrates how engineering can be directly applied to healthcare challenges that have historically received limited attention. The women of InnovateNaija tackled broad issues across multiple sectors. Elizabeth Chioma Chiketarauba of Imo State developed Torquenova , an electric vehicle and main power generator that can be recharged using an in-built solar-powered system or mains supply, bringing together mobility, energy, and renewable technology. Rita Idehai of Edo State developed an Automated Reverse Vending Machine, applying technology to waste management and environmental sustainability. Chinyere Esther Onwumel

Innovating Across Every Sector Akpagbula’s top finish was part of a larger showing by female innovators across the competition. Among the seven female finalists was Kemisola Bolarinwa from Ekiti State, whose innovation, the Smart Bra Cup Diagnostic Device , explores the use of technology in breast health. Her work demonstrates how engineering can be directly applied to healthcare challenges that have historically received limited attention. The women of InnovateNaija tackled broad issues across multiple sectors. Elizabeth Chioma Chiketarauba of Imo State developed Torquenova , an electric vehicle and main power generator that can be recharged using an in-built solar-powered system or mains supply, bringing together mobility, energy, and renewable technology. Rita Idehai of Edo State developed an Automated Reverse Vending Machine, applying technology to waste management and environmental sustainability. Chinyere Esther Onwumelu of Nasarawa State created a Gas-Level Monitoring and Community Gas Metering System , addressing energy access and accountability. Khadija Adamu Dandad a of Kano State developed the Shepall App , demonstrating the role digital solutions can play in addressing practical everyday needs. Miriam Ashiemar Agbo of Benue State created the Anatsor Integrated Poultry Management System , applying technology to agricultural productivity and livestock management. And Adaeze Ruth Akpagbula of Abia State developed PenKeep , advancing smart poultry climate control and ultimately earning the top spot on the national stage. A Technology Story That Includes Women Their stories matter far beyond the competition itself. Nigeria’s technology sector needs innovators who can identify problems, build solutions, and take concepts from an idea to a tangible product. The presence and eventual victory of female innovators among the InnovateNaija finalists provides a clear reminder that Nigerian women are already contributing to high-impact innovation. These finalists are engineers, inventors, developers, and problem-solvers. Their innovations span different sectors, states, and use cases. What connects them is not simply the problems they are solving, but the fact that they are building solutions themselves. Creating Room for the Next Generation of Women Builders Platforms such as InnovateNaija play an important role in creating more room for this kind of innovation. Led by NASENI alongside AfriLabs and the Federal Ministry of Youth Development, the challenge gave grassroots innovators a national stage to showcase their work and access opportunities for funding, technical expertise, manufacturing support, and scale. Beyond the cash prizes, which included a ₦100 million grand prize alongside ₦30 million and ₦20 million grants for the runners-up, all 15 finalists gained long-term access to advanced manufacturing tools and infrastructure across NASENI’s nationwide technology institutes. Most importantly, Adaeze Akpagbula’s victory and the work of her fellow female finalists give young Nigerian girls something tangible to see. A student with an idea can look at InnovateNaija and see that she does not have to wait for someone else to build the future. She can build it herself, and she can win. item.title: In space, 'We've gone from exploration to exploitation,' says original Voyager team member
item.description: It's been nearly half a century since the Voyager probes launched from Earth on a mission to explore the outer solar system, and they're still running. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify , Apple Podcasts , or YouTube . You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live. You're probably familiar with some of Voyager's iconic images, like the Pale Blue Dot and and its portraits of the outer planets. Those photos and observations wouldn't have been possible without Voyager's imaging team, eight members of which were selected from scientists from around the world. The UK's sole representative, Dr. Garry Hunt, joins us on this episode of The Kettle to discuss his role in the Voyager program, the future of the mission, and the state of science in the UK, US, and beyond. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:01) Hi everyone, and welcome to another episode of The Register ’s Kettle Podcast. I'm your host, Brandon Vigliarolo, and we have a very special episode for you this week. We're gonna step away from the doom and gloom of AI and the silliness of Silicon Valley to talk about something and to someone of considerably more historic importance. The Voyager space missions will mark fifty years of exploring the solar system and beyond next year. With us to talk about this is Reg Reporter Richard Speed and our very special guest, British astrophysicist Dr. Garry Hunt who was a member of the original Voyager imaging team. Thank you so much, Dr. Hunt, for coming on. And I'm gonna turn this over to Richard today, since you two have such a history together working on stories for The Reg , and I'm excited to hear about what he's going to pick your brain about. So Richard, take it away. item.dc:creator: Brandon Vigliarolo
item.content:encoded: It's been nearly half a century since the Voyager probes launched from Earth on a mission to explore the outer solar system, and they're still running. You can listen to the latest episode of The Kettle on this page, Spotify , Apple Podcasts , or YouTube . You can also subscribe on those platforms to be notified when a new episode goes live. You're probably familiar with some of Voyager's iconic images, like the Pale Blue Dot and and its portraits of the outer planets. Those photos and observations wouldn't have been possible without Voyager's imaging team, eight members of which were selected from scientists from around the world. The UK's sole representative, Dr. Garry Hunt, joins us on this episode of The Kettle to discuss his role in the Voyager program, the future of the mission, and the state of science in the UK, US, and beyond. A lightly edited transcript is included below: Brandon (00:01) Hi everyone, and welcome to another episode of The Register ’s Kettle Podcast. I'm your host, Brandon Vigliarolo, and we have a very special episode for you this week. We're gonna step away from the doom and gloom of AI and the silliness of Silicon Valley to talk about something and to someone of considerably more historic importance. The Voyager space missions will mark fifty years of exploring the solar system and beyond next year. With us to talk about this is Reg Reporter Richard Speed and our very special guest, British astrophysicist Dr. Garry Hunt who was a member of the original Voyager imaging team. Thank you so much, Dr. Hunt, for coming on. And I'm gonna turn this over to Richard today, since you two have such a history together working on stories for The Reg , and I'm excited to hear about what he's going to pick your brain about. So Richard, take it away. Richard Speed (00:46) Well Dr. Hunt, we've spoken a lot about the Voyager project over the years, but for anyone who's not aware of it, I wonder if you could summarize the mission, which is, I know, a big ask, and also what your role in it is and was. Garry Hunt (01:00) Well indeed, it's a unique mission in the sense that every 176 years the major planets Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, line up virtually in a straight line. And we wanted to explore the outer planets 'cause we've never been there before. I'm talking in the 1970s, late 1960s, '70s. So this is an unknown world. We thought that the major planets were keys to understanding the origin of the solar system, indeed the origin of life, so sending space missions there was a priority. But it needed to be done in a very economical way. With the planets lined up, that meant we could get there in the quickest way, requiring less fuel, and it would be the best way of going about it. So the opportunity came and NASA funded a mission to send two spacecraft at this unique time, which was in the mid '70s, 1977, to the major planets. NASA sent out an invitation to tender. They selected the ten instruments. Imaging had as an instrument in concept had been suggested, but they wanted a team of real scientists, not astronomers, not basic astronomers. They understood this is a chance to do real detailed science, real physics, real chemistry, the whole understanding of what went on. So they were looking for an interdisciplinary group of people. They selected eight people from invitations and I gather there were about nearly a thousand people proposed and of those eight I was chosen. Brandon (02:43) Wow. Garry Hunt (02:44) So I decided I suddenly found myself in this incredible position. I'm there to represent atmospheric physics. I want to understand the physics, the meteorology of the major planets. So here is an opportunity to explore the outer planets to learn about why we wanted to go to Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. However, funding was tight. The president at the time was Nixon, and we only had funding as far as Jupiter and Saturn. So we were treading new territory. At the time the mission was sort of decided, we had not been through the asteroid belt. So the first question was: would the spacecraft even get that far? And of course the Pioneers had just been launched at the beginning of the '70s and they managed to get through and raised a lot of questions. So I was part of the imaging team, this amazing set of what I will call prima donnas, because we all were. They were from Carl Sagan to Vern Suomi, who was a meteorologist, to Brad Smith, a whole collection of people. And we had to design the imaging system, the cameras, and be part of the organization that developed the choice of trajectories and all the other facets of this mission. In other words, we had to understand the risks as well as the potential rewards that came from it. So it was a big responsibility. And to put the whole thing in real context, I learnt in December '72 from NASA that I'd been selected. We had our first mission meetings in February of '73, and we had until the summer of 1977 to get the spacecraft launched. And the window for launching was ten days. So this was really a big precision job. So large responsibility and had many opportunities, not only to do the science, but the work that I was doing when I took the data back to the UK was to actually serve as a trigger for planetary research within the UK. So this really was a major major part of a new world, new understanding. And as we have learned over the years, we have made history and just about all the observations we've made. Richard Speed (05:16) Okay, great, thank you. So, I mean, as you said, it's been coming out for half a century, 50 years since the spacecraft were launched on their mission and they've been, as you say, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune, and so on. I was just wondering, why do you think they've lasted for so long? Because it's just incredible, really if you think about it. Garry Hunt (05:36) Well, firstly I will put my hand up and say that the engineers of JPL are exceptional. We've had a few hitches and they've overcome it. First of all, we also said we want a spacecraft. It's going to unknown territories. We don't know how long it's going to last. Reliability was the key. So it was built around the Mariners, which have been the bedrock of the earlier missions to around Mars and flying by Venus. So that was the first thing. And so many of the aspects of it were built from equipment from the mid-sixties. So the issue is even more exciting to think that here we are 50 years after launch flying a spacecraft with equipment which was already 10 years old by the time we got it there. So this really is an example of reliability, which is the bottleneck. And of course, the other aspect of it we built in redundancy as well. So we knew that, if things went wrong, we had to find a way of easily overcoming it. As it's drifting away at the speed of thirty thousand miles an hour, you can't just sort of go out and repair it. You've got to be able to do things while the spacecraft is in motion. So there's a certain amount of redundancy, built in reliability, incredibly good careful planning, absolutely brilliant engineers who to this day are doing the most incredible things. Richard Speed (07:05) Well, yes, I have to say, I agree, having spoken to the current Voyager team, they are a bunch of very impressive individuals. And they seem to keep eking out more and more life from the spacecraft. I know it's powered by RTGs, which will eventually expire and there won't be enough power to keep it going. But it seems they'll be able to continue well into the 2030s, maybe even beyond. I mean, what do you think is going to end the mission because I mean it must be coming up. Do you think it'll be a hardware failure? We have had some spacecraft failures over the years or do you think it's going to be more prosaic? Perhaps it'll be just a lack of funding. Garry Hunt (07:41) Well, if you go back to our elementary school physics, we know that as it moves away the signal strength di

item.title: 5 New Music Videos You Need to Watch This Week: Victony, Tyla, Phyno & More
item.description: Nigerian singer-songwriter Victony wearing a glossy leather outfit on set during the production of the SLICK Remix, featuring American stars Don Toliver and Summer Walker, off his sophomore album STARLIFE. A new week calls for fresh music, and there’s plenty to add to your watchlist. From Victony bringing Don Toliver and Summer Walker into the mix for the “ SLICK ” remix to Tyla ’s dance-ready “ That Girl ” and Phyno ’s romantic “Beautiful”, there’s something for every mood. We’re also looking back at Ayra Starr ’s performance at the 2026 NFL international halftime show and making room for Anendlessocean ’s reflective “ Promises ”. Here are five music releases and performances to check out this week. Victony: “SLICK (Remix)” ft. Don Toliver & Summer Walker Victony has given “SLICK” a new twist, and this time, he’s brought Don Toliver and Summer Walker along for the ride. The original track appears on his sophomore album, STARLIFE, while the remix introduces a fresh mix of R&B vocals and melodies. With three artistes bringing their different sounds to the same record, there’s plenty to enjoy here. Tyla: “That Girl” If you’re looking for something to get you moving, Tyla has you covered with “That Girl” from her project A*Pop. The song draws on South Africa’s popular Phara Walk dance culture, pairing catchy rhythms with Tyla’s smooth vocals. It’s playful, danceable and one you might find yourself returning to throughout the week. Anendlessocean: “Promises” Anendlessocean offers a place for reflection, gratitude and rest with “Promises”. Rooted in faith and the assurance that God will come through again, the song invites listeners to pause, reflect and find comfort in the belief that He will do it again. It’s one to turn to when you need a little reminder to trust the journey. Phyno: “Beautiful” Ezege is back with “Beautiful”, a love letter to the woman who makes everything make sense. Smooth, heartfelt and unmistakably Phyno, the track blends Igbo, Pidgin and English over a melody made for the ones you hold close. Taken from his project Let That Sink In (LTSI), the song celebrates love in a way that feels personal and familiar. The official music video features actress and media personality Nancy Isime, giving the romantic track a visual companion. Ayra Starr: 2026 NFL Halftime Performance Ayra Starr took Afrobeats to the NFL international stage on 11 October, headlining the halftime show during the Philadelphia Eagles vs Jacksonville Jaguars game at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium in London. She opened her set with “Heaven Baby”, her collaboration with ZAYN, before performing “Santa”, “Rush” and “Dangerous”, and closing with a medley of “Hot Body” and “Ms. Paper”. The performance marked a major milestone for the Nigerian star, who became the first African artiste to headline an NFL International Games halftime show. item.title: Museum exhibit reveals the intricate workings of a knackered Dell
item.description: Today's entry in the catalog of bork comes from Coventry's Herbert Art Gallery & Museum, where an information terminal is showing more about the hardware behind the scenes than the objects on display. Register reader Jeffrey Borinsky spotted the panel, which should have demonstrated a Jacquard loom in action but was instead displaying a warning about its host PC's failing battery. The Jacquard loom was a clever device dating back to the dawn of the 19th century. It used punched cards to control a loom's weaving patterns. The result was complicated and repeatable textile designs that reduced the need for skilled humans. Register readers of a certain age are doubtless nodding sagely at the mention of punched cards, which would go on to become foundational in the world of computing. Borinsky reported that several screens at the museum were in distress. Ribbon weaving was Coventry's main industry from the early 1700s until the 1860s, so a demonstration of Jacquard weaving fits right in, even if the bleating about the BIOS battery was probably not what Joseph Jacquard had in mind. The device running behind the scenes is a Dell OptiPlex 755, likely from around 2007. Not quite centuries old like a Jacquard loom, but certainly getting on a bit in the IT world. The first iPhone arrived in 2007, and a PC of a similar vintage likely shipped with Windows XP or Windows Vista. The CMOS battery is on the way out. Dell specifies a CR2032 coin cell, so replacement should be straightforward after disconnecting the power and taking anti-static precautions. Rather less traumatic than the head-in-hands moment when a retro enthusiast discovers a leaking battery has eaten through delicate circuit traces. A fresh battery and restored BIOS settings should be enough to get the loom demonstration weaving again. Given how important punched cards became in the history of computing, we'd recommend visiting anywhere that shows how a Jacquard loom operated. At least it didn't need a battery-backed BIOS to do its thing. ®

item.title: Watch Japan launch a bold sample-return mission to Mars moon Phobos today
item.description: null Editor's note: Japan launched its bold MMX sample-return mission to the Mars moon Phobos on Oct. 19) at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT). Watch a replay of the liftoff and read our launch story here. Japan will launch an epic mission to Mars today (Oct. 19), and you can watch the action live. The Martian Moons eXploration ( MMX ) mission is scheduled to lift off atop an H3 rocket from Japan's Tanegashima Space Center today at 3:41 p.m. EDT (1941 GMT; 4:41 a.m. on Oct. 20 local Japan time). You can watch it live via the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Coverage will begin at 2:45 p.m. EDT (1845 GMT). An artist’s concept of JAXA’s MMX spacecraft during its Mars orbit insertion. The Martian moon Phobos, which MMX will explore and sample, is in the background. (Image credit: JAXA) As its full name suggests, MMX will focus on Mars ' two moons, Phobos and Deimos . They're both tiny compared to Earth's own moon; Phobos is just 14 miles (22 kilometers) wide, and Deimos is even smaller, with a diameter of about 8 miles (13 km). They're also quite mysterious. While astronomers have a pretty clear understanding of our own moon's birth — it coalesced from material blasted into space when a Mars-sized planet slammed into Earth long ago — there's no consensus about Phobos and Deimos' origin story. The duo "may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA Headquarters, said in an Oct. 15 statement . (NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.) "Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added. MMX will help provide that answer, if all goes according to plan. The spacecraft will arrive in the Mars system in August 2027, then slip into orbit around Phobos a month later. It will study that moon and Deimos from a distance for about 18 months, then deploy the French-German Idefix rover onto Phobos' surface in early 2029. The 55-pound (25 kilograms) Idefix "has two main tasks: providing information to prepare for the landing of the main spacecraft to collect samples, and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos' surface," European Space Agency officials wrote in an MMX mission description . "The gravity on Phobos is so low that Idefix will only weigh the equivalent of 15 grams [0.5 ounces] on its surface!" they added. The MMX mothership's Phobos landing will occur in 2030. The spacecraft will grab at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples from the moon, then head back toward Earth with this extraterrestrial bounty. MMX's return capsule will land here in 2031, after which scientists around the world w

(NASA is a partner on the mission, providing a scientific instrument, a technology demonstration, communication support and funding for American scientists on the MMX team.) "Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds," Statler added. It will study that moon and Deimos from a distance for about 18 months, then deploy the French-German Idefix rover onto Phobos' surface in early 2029. The 55-pound (25 kilograms) Idefix "has two main tasks: providing information to prepare for the landing of the main spacecraft to collect samples, and analyzing the composition and texture of Phobos' surface," European Space Agency officials wrote in an MMX mission description . "The gravity on Phobos is so low that Idefix will only weigh the equivalent of 15 grams [0.5 ounces] on its surface!" they added. The MMX mothership's Phobos landing will occur in 2030. The spacecraft will grab at least 10 grams (0.4 ounces) of samples from the moon, then head back toward Earth with this extraterrestrial bounty. MMX's return capsule will land here in 2031, after which scientists around the world will scrutinize the Phobos sample for clues about the history and evolution of Mars and our solar system more broadly. Engineers conduct a thermal vacuum test with JAXA's MMX Mars moon sample-return spacecraft. JAXA posted this image on X on May 15, 2025. (Image credit: JAXA) MMX was originally supposed to launch in 2024, but issues with the H3 rocket prevented it from doing so. Mars and Earth align properly for interplanetary launches just once every 26 months, so MMX had to wait a while for its next chance. Japan already has an impressive sample-return track record. The country's Hayabusa mission brought home pieces of the asteroid Itokawa in 2010, for example, and Hayabusa2 did the same with material from the space rock Ryugu a decade later.

item.title: Microsoft’s second-hand licensing appeal gets the brush-off
item.description: Microsoft has failed to win permission to appeal to the UK Supreme Court in the long-running legal spat with ValueLicensing after the Court of Appeal refused its application. The US megacorp was challenging a November 2025 ruling in ValueLicensing's favor that VL may resell pre-owned software licenses. That judgment was unambiguous, but Microsoft told The Register at the time that it would seek permission to appeal. That request was rejected last week in blunt terms. No reasons were given for the refusal, just the words "It is ordered that the application is refused." It isn't quite the end of the road. Microsoft could apply to the Supreme Court itself, but it would need to file within 28 days and show a compelling reason why the Court of Appeal was wrong to refuse its appeal. Things are looking dicey for Microsoft in the case that started in 2021 when ValueLicensing sued Microsoft for £270 million over claims that the Windows maker choked off the supply of surplus Office licenses. Microsoft denied any wrongdoing and Instead attempted to reframe the case as a copyright dispute. The UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected Microsoft's arguments and a subsequent appeal. A recently published Consent Order adds to the pressure. It demands documents from past and present Microsoft bosses, including a potentially explosive internal deck titled "Second-Hand Software Presentation" (SHS). The contents of the file are unknown, but the Consent Order refers to it as a "Known Adverse Document." It dates back to 2013, a few years after Office 365 was launched. The order also asks why Microsoft waited until the end of 2025 to disclose the document’s existence, a few years after Office 365 launched. To add a little more spice, Alexander Wolfson is listed as an intervener on the appeal refusal. He is the proposed class representative in a separate claim filed on behalf of millions of UK customers seeking between £1.3 billion to £3.5 billion in compensation from Microsoft over its conduct regarding pre-owned licenses. ValueLicensing and Microsoft declined to comment on the latest development. Appeals aside, the next stage will be a Witness Statement from Microsoft explaining who knew what and when, followed by further disclosure. ®
item.dc:creator: Richard Speed
item.content:encoded: Microsoft has failed to win permission to appeal to the UK Supreme Court in the long-running legal spat with ValueLicensing after the Court of Appeal refused its application. The US megacorp was challenging a November 2025 ruling in ValueLicensing's favor that VL may resell pre-owned software licenses. That judgment was unambiguous, but Microsoft told The Register at the time that it would seek permission to appeal. That request was rejected last week in blunt terms. No reasons were given for the refusal, just the words "It is ordered that the application is refused." It isn't quite the end of the road. Microsoft could apply to the Supreme Court itself, but it would need to file within 28 days and show a compelling reason why the Court of Appeal was wrong to refuse its appeal. Things are looking dicey for Microsoft in the case that started in 2021 when ValueLicensing sued Microsoft for £270 million over claims that the Windows maker choked off the supply of surplus Office licenses. Microsoft denied any wrongdoing and Instead attempted to reframe the case as a copyright dispute. The UK's Competition Appeal Tribunal rejected Microsoft's arguments and a subsequent appeal. A recently published Consent Order adds to the pressure. It demands documents from past and present Microsoft bosses, including a potentially explosive internal deck titled "Second-Hand Software Presentation" (SHS). The contents of the file are unknown, but the Consent Order refers to it as a "Known Adverse Document." It dates back to 2013, a few years after Office 365 was launched. The order also asks why Microsoft waited until the end of 2025 to disclose the document’s existence, a few years after Office 365 launched. To add a little more spice, Alexander Wolfson is listed as an intervener on the appeal refusal. He is the proposed class representative in a separate claim filed on behalf of millions of UK customers seeking between £1.3 billion to £3.5 billion in compensation from Microsoft over its conduct regarding pre-owned licenses. ValueLicensing and Microsoft declined to comment on the latest development. Appeals aside, the next stage will be a Witness Statement from Microsoft explaining who knew what and when, followed by further disclosure. ®

item.title: AI’s epic cash call is matched only by its ability to strangle revenue streams
item.description: As it was written , so it has come to pass. A while back, we suggested that given how good AI was at code analysis, it would become possible to clone large applications. And then where would we be? Here, that’s where. An industrious individual has released source code and binaries for Claude-copied Microsoft Office and Adobe Creative Suite programs, disappointingly not calling elements of the latter Fauxtoshop . They’re in pre-alpha states of incomplete bugginess, but with substantial functionality, which is proof of how insanely productive AI can be given a task needing zero creativity and wearing "This is what a proof of concept looks like" and "Unintended Consquesences" T-shirts. They could also add Karma Police to their wardrobe. It’s clear that Microsoft and Adobe are facing some competition from what their rival describes as "clean-room reimplementations." It’s also unclear that there is any law against it. You can’t copyright functionality, the code has been generated in Rust with claimed clean-room conditions, and while there may be something in claiming that the works are substantially derivative, there’s a big problem here. Companies that sell AI trained on the biggest theft of IP in history are going to need unmatched legal dexterity to claim that AI shouldn’t be allowed to sully their own IP. Chutzpah used to be defined as a child on trial for murdering their parents begging for mercy on the grounds that they’re an orphan. We’ll have to update that. The post-codeclone world is going to be interesting. Everything becomes effectively open source, which closes down substantial revenue streams for big companies who had assumed lock-in. The motivation to build ab-initio alternatives may go away, in open source as well as closed. The push to subscription-only cloud-hosted products, where nobody can get their thieving AI prompts on binaries, seems an obvious counter move, but AI can control and scrape a web interface, which is all it needs. It's an arms race that won’t be won by humans. Code cloning is just the latest case of AI being so disruptive it threatens its creators. Another is the doom loop that Microsoft-OpenAI acknowledged in internal emails : by siphoning away the ad revenue that pays for content, AI chokes off the data it depends on. It's deforestation by companies that built their business on other people's IP. The biggest potential point of failure is the money.
