This is partly thanks to the surrounding mountains, which create a rain shadow effect, reducing the precipitation in the area. Glacial-carved valley Lapporten, in Abisko National Park. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) And if you're visiting Abisko, I'd highly recommend taking the chairlift up Mount Nuolja to the Aurora Sky Station . The views across Abisko National Park and the surrounding mountains are spectacular. Just be sure to check the chairlift's operating dates and times before visiting, as it doesn't run throughout the entire season. My tip: Although my two-night gamble paid off, I wouldn't recommend relying on such a short window if seeing the northern lights is your main goal. If possible, give yourself at least three or four nights to improve your chances of clear skies and aurora activity. Tromsø, Norway: Best for a city break Tromsø is the perfect destination for an aurora city break. (Image credit: Juan Maria Coy Vergara via Getty Images) Best time to visit: September to early April If you want to experience the northern lights without giving up the comforts of city life, Tromsø is hard to beat. Located high above the Arctic Circle in northern Norway, Tromsø sits beneath the auroral oval, the region surrounding Earth's magnetic poles where auroras occur most frequently. What I particularly like about Tromsø is that it offers the best of both worlds. You have a lively city with excellent restaurants, cafes, shops, museums and accommodation, while spectacular mountains and wilderness are only a short journey away. There's also a huge range of northern lights tours available, from small-group photography excursions to longer aurora-chasing adventures. My tip: Tromsø is ideal if you want to combine northern lights hunting with a city break holiday. I'd recommend booking at least one guided aurora tour, particularly if the local weather forecast looks challenging. The Norwegian coast: Best for a scenic Arctic voyage Northern lights during a cruise along the Norwegian coast with Hurtigruten. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) Best time to visit: September to March If there's one northern lights experience I'd encourage people to consider, it's sailing along the Norwegian coast. I've been fortunate enough to travel along this extraordinary coastline on several occasions , and there's something very special about watching the northern lights from the deck of a ship, surrounded by good company, mountains, fjords and the dark Arctic sea. Operators such as Hurtigruten and HX offer voyages along the Norwegian coast, combining opportunities to see the northern lights with some of the most spectacular scenery in Europe. While Hurtigruten operates coastal voyages calling at towns and communities along the route, HX offers expedition-style experiences with a focus on exploring the natural environment. Arctic Norway during the winter months offers truly stunning views. Photo captured during a Hurtigruten voyage. (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) Rather than staying in one location, you'll travel through different coastal landscapes, with opportunities to experience Arctic wildlife, local culture and winter excursions along the way. And then, of course, there's the possibility of the northern lights appearing overhead. Join me on a northern lights voyage! (Image credit: Daisy Dobrijevic) I'll be setting sail on a handful of Hurtigruten's astronomy voyages as a guest lecturer, sharing the science and wonder of the northern lights along the way. However, there's an important trade-off. Unlike a land-based aurora chase, a ship can't simply drive inland to escape coastal cloud cover. You're largely dependent on the weather along your route, although traveling through different regions over several nights gives you multiple opportunities. Hurtigruten also offers a Northern Lights Promise on qualifying voyages, providing a complimentary return voyage if the lights aren't officially sighted during your trip. Be sure to check the eligibility requirements and terms before booking. My tip: Choose a Norwegian coastal voyage because you want to experience the coastline itself. The scenery, communities and Arctic landscapes make it a remarkable journey regardless of auroras. Finnish Lapland: Best for a winter wonderland getaway Best time to visit: September to March If you dream of a northern lights holiday involving snow-covered forests, cozy cabins and perhaps even watching auroras from a glass-roofed igloo, Finnish Lapland could be the perfect choice. Northern Finland lies beneath the auroral oval, making it a popular destination for aurora chasers. Places such as Inari, Saariselkä and Ivalo offer excellent access to dark skies and Arctic wilderness. Rovaniemi, the official hometown of Santa Claus, is another popular option, particularly for families, although it's worth traveling away from the city's lights for the best views. My tip: For a quieter, more wilderness-focused escape, I'd look at northern Lapland around Inari or Saariselkä. If you're traveling with children or want a more activity-packed holiday, Rovaniemi may be a better fit. item.title: Football Daily | Watford, a ‘fake news’ sacking and an apology to Elton John
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! There are only two things certain in life – death and taxes Reece James knack and Watford managerial news – and Football Daily’s bingo card lit up with both on Friday. But while Chelsea’s statement on their crocked right-back having successful knee surgery was a cut-and-paste job from the last time James was injured, the quotes by Watford manager Alessio Dionisi were much more exciting, mainly because it contained an actual apology to Elton John and the remarkable news that the club’s trigger-happy owners have not already sent the Italian the same way as an apple in Michael Owen’s house . Shall we just hand over the Bigger Cup to PSG now to ease the calendar congestion?” – Krishna Moorthy. Reading that ‘European football leaders are increasingly confident they will find a candidate to stand against Infantino next year’ , I can’t be the only well informed reader to think that a certain intergalactic bin wearing member of the nobility would make a terrific candidate. Can the Big Website ‘Higher Ups’ have a word?!” – Chris Reid. Looking at the Benfica v Celtic game I was immediately drawn to the presence of two Durans. Have there been any other instances of any other bands being present in a game? Possibly in the Human League? I am hoping a Serie A game with a Scritti and a Politti … a French game with Depeche and Mode. You get the general idea” – Mike Turney. Continue reading...

item.title: Beyond pointing your phone at the night sky, this is how to use stargazing apps effectively
item.description: Whether you are a seasoned astronomer or a newcomer to the hobby, the best stargazing apps have the potential to seriously enhance your skywatching experience. But it's easy to overlook just how useful these portable programs can be. That's why we've put together this guide to getting the best use out of stargazing apps, from identifying stars and constellations through to seeking out dark sky sites and beyond. You will wonder how you ever managed without them. So read on and get ready to take your stargazing to the next level. And if you're wondering how else technology can take the work out of skywatching, we've also rounded up the best smart telescopes . Using stargazing apps Some apps use Augmented Reality (AR) features to allow users to scan the sky in real-time. (Image credit: Getty Images) Before we explore specific uses, there are a few things you need to know about using the best stargazing apps on your Apple or Android device. Firstly, while some apps support offline use, you'll typically need a mobile or Wi-Fi signal with data to make the most of these apps. Also, some apps lock certain features behind a paywall. Pay for Stellarium Plus, for example, and you get an additional 2 million deep sky objects, the ability to connect to certain telescopes and more. Finally, while many stargazing apps are relatively intuitive, we'd recommend you familiarize yourself with them at home before taking them out into the field. Identifying stars in the field Sky Tonight is one of the apps that, via AR, can be used to identify stars and other objects. (Image credit: Vito Technology) One of the most common and convenient uses for stargazing apps is identifying stars, constellations and more, just by pointing your phone's camera at them. It really is that simple. Take Sky Tonight , which we think is the best stargazing app for AR (augmented reality). Launch the app, grant it camera access and turn it towards the object you want to identify. The name will appear on screen and you can also tap to learn more about it, whether it's a star, constellation, planet or nebula. Conversely, you can also use the app to find specific objects in the sky. Want to view Uranus at opposition this Nov. 25 but aren't sure where to look? Search for it in Sky Tonight and the app will point you to it. (Image credit: Future) Being able to identify night sky objects in the field is a real boon, but what if you've already taken a photograph and want to identify which stars were visible? item.dc:creator: Chris McMullen
item.content:encoded: Whether you are a seasoned astronomer or a newcomer to the hobby, the best stargazing apps have the potential to seriously enhance your skywatching experience. But it's easy to overlook just how useful these portable programs can be. That's why we've put together this guide to getting the best use out of stargazing apps, from identifying stars and constellations through to seeking out dark sky sites and beyond. You will wonder how you ever managed without them. So read on and get ready to take your stargazing to the next level. And if you're wondering how else technology can take the work out of skywatching, we've also rounded up the best smart telescopes . Using stargazing apps Some apps use Augmented Reality (AR) features to allow users to scan the sky in real-time. (Image credit: Getty Images) Before we explore specific uses, there are a few things you need to know about using the best stargazing apps on your Apple or Android device. Firstly, while some apps support offline use, you'll typically need a mobile or Wi-Fi signal with data to make the most of these apps. Also, some apps lock certain features behind a paywall. Pay for Stellarium Plus, for example, and you get an additional 2 million deep sky objects, the ability to connect to certain telescopes and more. Finally, while many stargazing apps are relatively intuitive, we'd recommend you familiarize yourself with them at home before taking them out into the field. Identifying stars in the field Sky Tonight is one of the apps that, via AR, can be used to identify stars and other objects. (Image credit: Vito Technology) One of the most common and convenient uses for stargazing apps is identifying stars, constellations and more, just by pointing your phone's camera at them. It really is that simple. Take Sky Tonight , which we think is the best stargazing app for AR (augmented reality). Launch the app, grant it camera access and turn it towards the object you want to identify. The name will appear on screen and you can also tap to learn more about it, whether it's a star, constellation, planet or nebula. Conversely, you can also use the app to find specific objects in the sky. Want to view Uranus at opposition this Nov. 25 but aren't sure where to look? Search for it in Sky Tonight and the app will point you to it. Identifiying stars from photographs Sky Walk 2 lets you rewind and advance time, showing you where stars and other objects were or will be on that date. (Image credit: Future) Being able to identify night sky objects in the field is a real boon, but what if you've already taken a photograph and want to identify which stars were visible? That's where apps like Sky Walk 2 come in. If possible, you should return to the location where the photograph was taken, but if that's not possible, you can input GPS co-ordinates and Sky Walk 2 will show you the view from that location. Next, using the clock icon and slider, alter the date to the exact time you took the photograph (or as near as possible). You will then be shown the night sky as it was at the time. You can now tap on the star or stars you want to identify and Sky Walk 2 will tell you the name. Sky Walk 2 isn't the only app to offer such a facility, but in Sky Walk 2's case this feature is present in the free version of the app. Finding dark sky sites As Earth's population continues to grow, so does the problem of light pollution, so seeking out dark sky sites is essential for the best experience. (Image credit: Inigo Cia via Getty Images) It's a sad fact that light pollution has made it harder for astronomers to study the night sky. While the planets in our solar system are still visible, sky glow obscures more distant objects, such as fainter stars. You could travel to a dark sky reserve but, with the aid of one of several stargazing apps, it is also possible to find dark sky sites closer to home. Apps like Sky Safari and the simply named Light Pollution Map will show you the light pollution levels locally and globally, estimated on the Bortle scale. The latter app colors the map, with pink the most light pollution and black the least. In just a few seconds you can find out how light polluted your local area is, and use the map to find a location nearby where the sky is dark, or at least darker. Planning a stargazing trip Sky Safari 7 Pro is a stargazing app that will help you choose what you want to see and where. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Are you planning a stargazing trip? Then you'll be happy to hear there's an app for that. There are several, in fact, but Sky Safari has all you need to plan your next outing. You can create observation lists, find out when and where objects are visible, and while it won't book your tickets for you, it comes close. Our reviewer Jamie Carter used the app to plan his observations of conjunctions, specific moon views and astrophotography opportunities. Coupled with its light pollution map, it will be a huge help in putting together an itinerary for your skywatching trip. Troubleshooting stargazing apps Hopefully you'll have a smooth experience, but if you're having issues, here are a few things to try. Take your phone out of its case. Magnetic clasps can interfere with internal sensors. Make sure location services are enabled . Many apps use GPS to show you the correct view. Check your phone's clock. If your clock is not set accurately, apps may display an incorrect sky Swoop your phone in a figure eight motion. This can help calibrate your phone's "compass". Make sure you have a signal, and that data is enabled. Unless the app has an offline mode you will still need a connection. Signal may be poor at dark sky sites. Check each app's permissions . Location aside, Augmented Reality (AR) stargazing apps will need camera access. We've got you covered with reviews and rankings of the best telescopes , binoculars , star projectors , cameras , drones , Lego , streaming and more.

item.title: Supermassive black hole blasts out a neon 'treble clef' | Space photo of the day for Oct. 16, 2026
item.description: null The "treble clef" galaxy cluster is an unusual source of radio waves, the Chandra X-ray observatory has found. (Image credit: X-ray: NASA/CXC/INAF-IRA/A. Botteon et al.; Infrared: UKIDSS-GPS ; Radio: ASTRON/LOFAR; Image processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/N. Wolk) What looks like a neon pink treble clef floating out in space is actually a bizarre source of radio waves spotted deep in the cosmos. What is it? Scientists using NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory have peered far out into space to look at strange radio waves coming from what they have nicknamed the "treble clef" because of its distinct shape, which looks a lot like the musical notation. Using Chandra, as well as the German Extended RÖntgen Survey with an Imaging Telescope Array ( eROSITA ) X-ray telescope, researchers looking at this strange sight spotted a big cloud of blue gas, which we can see in this image, along with radio signals (seen here in bright pink). They think that this object is actually a huge galaxy cluster made up of two different clusters that are in the process of merging. Why is it incredible? The researchers think they may have gotten to the bottom of where these radio waves are coming from, they report in a new study. The team thinks that the treble clef-shaped radio signals were created by an outburst from a supermassive black hole . They believe that this outburst pushed clouds of charged particles and magnetic fields away from the galaxy cluster's center, producing bright radio waves. According to the scientists, following this bright outburst, there was likely an extreme collision between two galaxy clusters. This cosmic smash-up either compressed or somehow reenergized these charged particles to amplify the radio signal. When we see beautiful images of objects in space such as this, they can seem just like peaceful, colorful, cosmic clouds. But when you look a bit deeper, these spectacular scenes can actually be evidence of violent, chaotic events. This work was described in a study published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.

item.title: 'We are getting a lot of pressure from the administrator himself': How NASA is racing to obey Trump's 'Super Intelligence' order
item.description: null NASA has begun replacing references to artificial intelligence with "super intelligence" following an executive order from President Donald Trump, which directs government agencies not to acknowledge the terminology change in their external communications. An internal NASA document obtained by Space.com lays out plans to update the agency's websites, publications, organizational titles and digital infrastructure with a four-phase "super intelligence" implementation schedule extending into December. And the changes go beyond NASA's public-facing communications, with at least one planned technical update described as "a breaking change" expected to disrupt existing software integrations. The terminology shift arrives as NASA continues expanding its use of AI across missions and research programs, from autonomous Mars rover navigation to models capable of analyzing enormous amounts of scientific data. The technologies themselves aren't changing, but NASA's effort to implement the nomenclature introduces new obstacles for scientific communication and the agency's digital infrastructure. Trump's executive order (EO), called " Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence ," was signed on Sept. 29. It directs federal agencies to replace any mention of "artificial intelligence" and "AI" with "super intelligence" and "SI" in all official government communications. The White House argues that AI has advanced beyond simple automation or imitations of human intelligence, and that language befitting "a new era of Super Intelligence" is needed to better reflect the technology's emerging capabilities . Despite introducing the new name, the order retains the federal government's existing definition of artificial intelligence, which broadly covers machine-based learning systems capable of making predictions, recommendations or decisions. That means technologies already classified as AI can now be designated "super intelligence" without demonstrating any additional capabilities. To follow suit, NASA's Office of Communications (OCOMM) and Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) distributed an internal implementation schedule that outlines the span of work that the agency's multiple comms teams now have ahead of them. "Effective immediately, we must use "super intelligence" and "SI" in all in-scope content/publications," the document says, bolding the key terms. It covers both internal and external communications and instructs NASA employees to use "super intelligence" and "SI" in all new "presentations, exhibits, printed materials, media interviews, or other collateral or content for external audiences." Internally, the policy applies to all official employee communications, NASA style guides, intra-agency websites and IT systems referenced in public-facing communications or official materials. item.content:encoded: null NASA has begun replacing references to artificial intelligence with "super intelligence" following an executive order from President Donald Trump, which directs government agencies not to acknowledge the terminology change in their external communications. An internal NASA document obtained by Space.com lays out plans to update the agency's websites, publications, organizational titles and digital infrastructure with a four-phase "super intelligence" implementation schedule extending into December. And the changes go beyond NASA's public-facing communications, with at least one planned technical update described as "a breaking change" expected to disrupt existing software integrations. The terminology shift arrives as NASA continues expanding its use of AI across missions and research programs, from autonomous Mars rover navigation to models capable of analyzing enormous amounts of scientific data. The technologies themselves aren't changing, but NASA's effort to implement the nomenclature introduces new obstacles for scientific communication and the agency's digital infrastructure. Trump's executive order (EO), called " Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence ," was signed on Sept. 29. It directs federal agencies to replace any mention of "artificial intelligence" and "AI" with "super intelligence" and "SI" in all official government communications. The White House argues that AI has advanced beyond simple automation or imitations of human intelligence, and that language befitting "a new era of Super Intelligence" is needed to better reflect the technology's emerging capabilities . Despite introducing the new name, the order retains the federal government's existing definition of artificial intelligence, which broadly covers machine-based learning systems capable of making predictions, recommendations or decisions. That means technologies already classified as AI can now be designated "super intelligence" without demonstrating any additional capabilities. To follow suit, NASA's Office of Communications (OCOMM) and Office of the Chief Information Officer (OCIO) distributed an internal implementation schedule that outlines the span of work that the agency's multiple comms teams now have ahead of them. "Effective immediately, we must use "super intelligence" and "SI" in all in-scope content/publications," the document says, bolding the key terms. It covers both internal and external communications and instructs NASA employees to use "super intelligence" and "SI" in all new "presentations, exhibits, printed materials, media interviews, or other collateral or content for external audiences." Internally, the policy applies to all official employee communications, NASA style guides, intra-agency websites and IT systems referenced in public-facing communications or official materials. And NASA's instructions echo Trump's directive forgoing any kind of transitional language. "NASA is … adopting the terminology ‘Super Intelligence’ as the agency continues to expand the use of these rapidly advancing technologies across its missions," agency officials told Space.com in an emailed statement. "NASA is already applying SI to advance mission planning , autonomous systems, scientific research, and the analysis of complex datasets." Orders from the top NASA's Mars rover Perserverance team began using a vision-based artificial intelligence system to plan safe driving routes on Mars without a human controller in December 2025. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/MSSS) Agency leadership has generally been aligned with the current administration's agenda, adjusting NASA's priorities to meet the president's goals when needed. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman has helped lead that charge since his appointment to the position in December 2025; he has been a champion of Trump's human spaceflight-heavy vision for the agency since his first day. That should come as no surprise; NASA is, after all, part of the executive branch, and the agency is obliged to abide by executive orders. But Isaacman's relationship with Trump is, perhaps, more visible than that of past NASA chiefs. The duo have shared several jovial public interactions, including an unexpected phone call from Trump during a press conference celebrating the launch of NASA's Roman Space Telescope on Aug. 30. One month later, Isaacman attended a White House luncheon with more than a dozen AI tech executives, on the same day that Trump signed his super intelligence EO. While he's not an AI company executive, Isaacman is a member of the tech-billionaire community. Before beginning his tenure at NASA, Isaacman founded and served as CEO for Shift4 Payments, a payment processing company. He used some of that fortune to charter a pair of private astronaut launches with SpaceX — Inspiration4 and Polaris Dawn , which were the first-ever all-civilian orbital spaceflight and the flight that featured the first-ever private spacewalk , respectively. "I was honored to have an opportunity to join that luncheon," Isaacman said when asked his opinion of AI during a post-launch press conference for the SpaceX Crew-13 astronaut mission on Oct. 1. By that point, he had already added the SI nomenclature to his lexicon. "I made clear when it was my turn to speak … I am the space guy here [not an 'AI' guy]," he added as a caveat, before saying that the "potential super intelligence has … [can] change the course of civilizations." Isaacman's embrace of the new lingo may be partially behind NASA's own accelerated efforts to bring the agency's comms in line with the administration's. One NASA employee told Space.com, "We are getting a lot of pressure from the administrator himself to act on this." Internal difficulties Beyond just substituting one term for the other, NASA personnel have been told not to acknowledge the previous nomenclature at all, including short-term phrases such as "SI, also/formerly known as AI." The changes extend to related terms such as "generative AI" becoming "generative SI," with NASA's guidance directing agency messaging away from "automation." They'll now put an emphasis on how today's technologies "amplify human ingenuity and unlock new forms of creativity," the NASA document says, quoting Trump's order. The use of the term "SI," and the direction not to use "AI," applies across all NASA's centers and mission directorates, including contractors and personnel at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is run by Caltech. Specific technical citations, like "machine learning," "large language models" and "chatbot," remain acceptable, but the new terminology may run the risk of carrying different meanings in different contexts. Technical exceptions aside, some at NASA responsible for implementing the changes think it may present more obstacles than expected. "There's concern that there's going to be a lot of confusion in the scientific community and in the general population," a NASA employee knowledgeable of the plan told Space.com, under the condition of anonymity. (Image credit: Space.com) In recordings of an internal NASA communications meeting obtained by Space.com, employees echoed the same concerns to their direct management and voiced some frustration over their inability to relay to the public that the changes are being made in the first place. "We're not even supposed to use AI as a term ... it's being talked about like Voldemort or Macbeth, with people calling it 'the technology that must not be named,'" the NASA employee said. "Super intelligence and artificial intelligence — they have two different meanings. They both are already separate things," one meeting participant said. "As a science communicator … I feel like it's our responsibility to raise our hand and say, 'Hey, this is going to confuse people. This doesn't make sense.'" item.title: He Wants AI Benchmarking To Be a Science, Not a Dark Art
item.description: Benchmarks are the rulers of AI, in both senses of the word. item.title: Rocket Lab pushes 1st launch of next-gen Neutron rocket to 2027
item.description: null We'll have to wait a bit longer to see Rocket Lab's next-gen launcher fly. The California-based company just announced that it's pushing the debut of its powerful, partially reusable Neutron rocket from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue. "We believe Neutron is going to be a game-changer, and taking the time now to solve these challenges means we're in a better position to deliver a rocket that's ready to meet the needs for the industry for years to come," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said in a video the company posted on YouTube late on Tuesday (Oct. 13). Beck explained the issue in depth in that seven-minute video. It concerns the cabon-fiber propellant domes in Neutron's first stage — the large caps for the vehicle's fuel tanks, which hold liquid oxygen and liquid methane. Rocket Lab makes the domes using an automated fiber placement machine, "which lays down the carbon with speed and accuracy," Beck said. The company noticed a problem, however, after curing a recently manufactured forward (front-facing) dome: Inspectors found some voids within the carbon-fiber layers. The voids "don't necessarily mean that the dome would fail in flight, but our practice is to proceed only when we believe the system has the appropriate margins," Beck said. "Possible success isn't our standard." After analysis and testing, Rocket Lab added some "mitigations" to the dome-manufacturing process — a tweak that has done the trick, according to Beck. "We've since run another carbon composite section called the aft dome through this new process, and I'm pleased to report that it has resulted in the highest quality carbon composite dome to date, and we've solved the problem," he said. Rocket Lab still needs to build a new forward dome, then cure and inspect it — steps that are expected to be complete by the end of the year, according to Beck. The company then needs to incorporate that hardware into a complete Neutron first stage, and then subject that stage to a battery of tests. If all goes to plan, that will all be done during the first quarter of 2027. "From there, we expect to be in good shape to share a new target launch date," Beck said. Artist's illustration of Neutron's first stage coming down for a landing on a ship at sea. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) The newly announced delay is the latest setback for Neutron, which Rocket Lab announced in 2021 . item.dc:creator: Mike Wall
item.content:encoded: null We'll have to wait a bit longer to see Rocket Lab's next-gen launcher fly. The California-based company just announced that it's pushing the debut of its powerful, partially reusable Neutron rocket from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue. "We believe Neutron is going to be a game-changer, and taking the time now to solve these challenges means we're in a better position to deliver a rocket that's ready to meet the needs for the industry for years to come," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said in a video the company posted on YouTube late on Tuesday (Oct. 13). Beck explained the issue in depth in that seven-minute video. It concerns the cabon-fiber propellant domes in Neutron's first stage — the large caps for the vehicle's fuel tanks, which hold liquid oxygen and liquid methane. Rocket Lab makes the domes using an automated fiber placement machine, "which lays down the carbon with speed and accuracy," Beck said. The company noticed a problem, however, after curing a recently manufactured forward (front-facing) dome: Inspectors found some voids within the carbon-fiber layers. The voids "don't necessarily mean that the dome would fail in flight, but our practice is to proceed only when we believe the system has the appropriate margins," Beck said. "Possible success isn't our standard." After analysis and testing, Rocket Lab added some "mitigations" to the dome-manufacturing process — a tweak that has done the trick, according to Beck. "We've since run another carbon composite section called the aft dome through this new process, and I'm pleased to report that it has resulted in the highest quality carbon composite dome to date, and we've solved the problem," he said. Rocket Lab still needs to build a new forward dome, then cure and inspect it — steps that are expected to be complete by the end of the year, according to Beck. The company then needs to incorporate that hardware into a complete Neutron first stage, and then subject that stage to a battery of tests. If all goes to plan, that will all be done during the first quarter of 2027. "From there, we expect to be in good shape to share a new target launch date," Beck said. Artist's illustration of Neutron's first stage coming down for a landing on a ship at sea. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) The newly announced delay is the latest setback for Neutron, which Rocket Lab announced in 2021 . Back then, the company — which also flies the workhorse Electron small-satellite launcher — targeted a 2024 debut for the 141-foot-tall (42 meters) Neutron, which features a reusable first stage. That timeline has been pushed back multiple times — to 2025, then to early 2026 and then, after a fuel tank ruptured during a pressure test , to late 2026. Rocket Lab has been been steadfast throughout, stressing that it will not rush the development of a vehicle that it sees as vital to its future success. "There's significant demand for what Neutron has to offer, including some new contracts we'll be able to talk about soon," Beck said in the video. "Those customers understand that a reliable rocket is far more valuable than an early one, and we're grateful for their trust."

item.title: WIMBIZ Marks 25 Years of Global Impact, and Unveils Anniversary Logo
item.description: 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Communications Chair, Funmi Onuma; Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Rolake Akinkugbe-Filani; WIMBIZ 25th Anniversary Committee Chair, Awuneba Ajumogobia; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Morin Desalu; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Ifeyinwa Ighodalo; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Adeola Azeez; Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Osayi Alile; 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Chair, Ronke Onadeko; Executive Director, WIMBIZ, Omowunmi Akingbohungbe; and 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Vice Chair, Yemisi Peters, during the WIMBIZ@25 Press Conference in Lagos on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Women in Management, Business and Public Service (WIMBIZ) has reaffirmed its commitment to advancing women’s leadership, strengthening women-led enterprises and expanding economic opportunities across Africa and globally as it celebrates 25 years of impact. The organisation made this commitment at a press conference held on Tuesday, 13 October 2026, at the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Innovation Centre in Lagos, where it unveiled its 25th anniversary logo and highlighted the strategic priorities of its forthcoming 25TH Annual Conference. WIMBIZ announced Bennedikter China Molokwu , DF. CIoD, a corporate governance and strategy professional, as Chairperson of the WIMBIZ 25th Annual Conference. A past President of the Chartered Institute of Directors Nigeria, Molokwu has served on more than 15 boards and brings decades of experience in corporate governance, risk management and women’s empowerment to the annual conference. The press conference brought together founders, members of the Board of Trustees, the 25th Anniversary Committee, the 2026 Conference Planning Committee, media representatives, and partners, including IWOSAN and the Enterprise Development Centre (EDC). Reflecting on the organisation’s 25-year journey, Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Rolake Akinkugbe-Filani emphasised that while significant progress has been made, the pace of change must accelerate. She said, “Women are certainly on track, but the reality is that the world is not.” She highlighted that, despite decades of advocacy and progress, women remain underrepresented in management and political leadership, reinforcing the urgency of collective action to close the gender gap. item.content:encoded: 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Communications Chair, Funmi Onuma; Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Rolake Akinkugbe-Filani; WIMBIZ 25th Anniversary Committee Chair, Awuneba Ajumogobia; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Morin Desalu; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Ifeyinwa Ighodalo; Co-Founder, WIMBIZ, Adeola Azeez; Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Osayi Alile; 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Chair, Ronke Onadeko; Executive Director, WIMBIZ, Omowunmi Akingbohungbe; and 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Vice Chair, Yemisi Peters, during the WIMBIZ@25 Press Conference in Lagos on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. Women in Management, Business and Public Service (WIMBIZ) has reaffirmed its commitment to advancing women’s leadership, strengthening women-led enterprises and expanding economic opportunities across Africa and globally as it celebrates 25 years of impact. The organisation made this commitment at a press conference held on Tuesday, 13 October 2026, at the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) Innovation Centre in Lagos, where it unveiled its 25th anniversary logo and highlighted the strategic priorities of its forthcoming 25TH Annual Conference. WIMBIZ announced Bennedikter China Molokwu , DF. CIoD, a corporate governance and strategy professional, as Chairperson of the WIMBIZ 25th Annual Conference. A past President of the Chartered Institute of Directors Nigeria, Molokwu has served on more than 15 boards and brings decades of experience in corporate governance, risk management and women’s empowerment to the annual conference. The press conference brought together founders, members of the Board of Trustees, the 25th Anniversary Committee, the 2026 Conference Planning Committee, media representatives, and partners, including IWOSAN and the Enterprise Development Centre (EDC). Reflecting on the organisation’s 25-year journey, Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Rolake Akinkugbe-Filani emphasised that while significant progress has been made, the pace of change must accelerate. She said, “Women are certainly on track, but the reality is that the world is not.” She highlighted that, despite decades of advocacy and progress, women remain underrepresented in management and political leadership, reinforcing the urgency of collective action to close the gender gap. WIMBIZ Board of Trustees member Osayi Alile reinforced the importance of collaboration in achieving this ambition, noting that advancing women’s leadership requires collective responsibility rather than isolated efforts. “Gender is not only nice to have. It is a strategic thing. It is an economic thing as well,” she emphasised, calling on stakeholders to recognise women’s participation as a critical driver of economic growth and sustainable development. WIMBIZ also called on the media to amplify the stories of women creating change, strengthen public awareness of gender inclusion and support the organisation’s efforts to expand opportunities for women in Nigeria, across Africa and globally. 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Communications Chair, Funmi Onuma; 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Vice Chair, Yemisi Peters; Chief Information Officer, IWOSAN, Olanrewaju Lawal; Group Head, Marketing & Growth, IWOSAN, Foluso Adeyemi; Member, WIMBIZ Board of Trustees, Osayi Alile; 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Chair, Ronke Onadeko; WIMBIZ 25th Anniversary Committee Chair, Awuneba Ajumogobia; Executive Director, WIMBIZ, Omowunmi Akingbohungbe; Representative, Enterprise Development Centre, Mayo Deji-Omotayo; and Project Support Manager, Enterprise Development Centre, Halima Rabiu, during the WIMBIZ@25 Press Conference in Lagos on Tuesday, October 13, 2026. A defining moment of the press conference was the unveiling of the WIMBIZ 25th anniversary logo by WIMBIZ 25th Anniversary Committee Chair, Awuneba Ajumogobia . The unveiling marked a celebration of the organisation’s legacy and a renewed commitment to creating meaningful, measurable impact for future generations of women. Speaking at the unveiling, Mrs Ajumogobia reflected on the significance of the milestone and the individual stories behind WIMBIZ’s collective achievements. “Behind every figure, behind every number, is a woman who has found her voice, who has taken her seat at the table, who has built her business, or who has reached back to lift another woman,” she said. She explained that the anniversary identity was built around the word impact, reflecting both the progress made over the past 25 years and the work that remains. The logo symbolises women standing together, supporting one another and ensuring that more women can lead and succeed. “A logo is a promise that you can see. I will say that we have been impacting women for 25 years. What comes next will be different,” Mrs Ajumogobia added. As part of this next chapter, WIMBIZ is placing greater emphasis on practical solutions to the barriers confronting women entrepreneurs. Access to finance remains a significant challenge for many women-owned businesses, limiting their ability to expand operations, attract investment, and compete in larger markets. Further details of its initiatives are expected to be announced at the Annual Conference. The press conference also spotlighted the WIMBIZ 25th Annual Conference, scheduled for 5–6 November 2026 at Eko Hotels & Suites, Lagos. The conference will convene women across business, management and public service to explore opportunities for growth, innovation, leadership and global relevance. Speaking on the vision behind the conference, 2026 WIMBIZ Conference Planning Group Chair, Ronke Onadeko , emphasised the importance of helping women move beyond participation to building and leading enterprises capable of competing on the global stage. She challenged women to think bigger, leverage strategic relationships and position themselves within Africa’s expanding economic value chains. “We are born in Africa, and we are built for the world,” she said, reinforcing the conference theme and the need for African women to recognise their capacity to create, lead and compete globally. The conference programme will address key issues affecting women’s economic advancement, including access to capital, business growth, investment readiness, the creative economy, intellectual property protection, health and wellbeing, and strategic networking. Participants will also have opportunities to engage with business experts through collaboration with the Enterprise Development Centre of Pan-Atlantic University and IWOSAN, which is expected to provide practical guidance across areas such as finance, logistics, and supply chain management. The conference will further explore how women can build globally competitive businesses, attract investment, access strategic networks and take advantage of emerging opportunities across Africa and beyond. The WIMBIZ 25th Annual Conference is proudly supported by FirstBank and Dentsu Agyle as Headline Partners, alongside a distinguished lineup of sponsors and partners. Another key announcement at the press conference was the 2026 WIMBIZ Impact Investment Opportunity, which will provide grants of up to ₦6 million and two solar power systems to support outstanding women entrepreneurs in the food and beverage, sustainability, and innovation sectors. Speaking about the conference, WIMBIZ Executive Director, Omowunmi Akingbohungbe , described the 25th anniversary as both a moment of reflection and an opportunity to renew the organisation’s ambition for women’s leadership. “Twenty-five years is a milestone; it is a moment of reflection and renewed ambition. At this milestone, we are celebrating women who are grounded in Africa, advancing with purpose, and equipped to compete and contribute globally,” she said. WIMBIZ invites delegates from across the world, corporate partners, and members of the media to join in marking this historic milestone and to be part of a conference that celebrates the legacy, resilience, and global impact of Africa

item.title: It's time to reassess the size of our solar system, scientists say
item.description: null Two leading space scientists say there is a need to redefine the edge of the solar system by presenting a theory which states that measurements of the Milky Way's gravitational field, including its dark matter, redraws the sun's frontier. That theory was put forward by Jim Green, former NASA chief scientist and past director of the space agency's Planetary Science Division, along with Ed Belbruno, a professor of mathematics at Yeshiva University and a senior research associate at Princeton University. The solar system's gravitational frontier extends to nearly 3.8 light-years from the sun , they contend, roughly 241,000 astronomical units (AU), a distance that brings the "edge" of the solar system to within the same scale as the separation between neighboring stars. The edge of our solar system may be defined not by a sharp boundary, but by a "complex dance among forces, energies and trajectories," they write. Green and Belbruno recently made their case in the August 2026 issue of the magazine ROOM - the Space Journal of Asgardia. Slow moving objects Moreover, this theory claims that the gravitationally stable Solar Lagrange points L1 and L2 could form a type of "portal" that could funnel future interstellar visitors such as the recent comet 3I/ATLAS into the solar system, perhaps allowing scientists to capture them for future study. "Discovering the solar-galactic center L1 location is important since slow moving objects that enter this region can be captured by our sun and become part of our solar system," Green told Space.com. "Who knows if there may be a large captured rogue planet on its way into the solar system right now," he said. Green said there's a need to look at these newly calculated L1 and L2 locations to see what could be found. He is now in discussion about making such observations with the New Horizons spacecraft team that explored Pluto in 2015 and is now operating in the outer heliosphere. "Even accumulated dust in this region could verify many of the calculations we have made including the extent of the dark matter in our galaxy," said Green. A diagram showing the Lagrange points L1 though L5. (Image credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio) Ballistic capture "It's a really nice and significant result," Belbruno told Space.com. The ROOM article, written for a popular audience, draws from his August 2025 keynote lecture at the Niels Bohr Institute. Much of the theory also stems from Belbruno's work on permanent capture into the solar system and weak stability boundaries published in 2024 in the journal Celestial Mechanics and Dynamical Astronomy. Belbruno authored the book Fly Me to the Moon: An Insider's Guide to the New Science of Space Travel (Princeton University Press, Princeton, 2007). In that work, he spells out how to harness low-fuel space travel he likens to "surfing the gravitational field." item.content:encoded: null Two leading space scientists say there is a need to redefine the edge of the solar system by presenting a theory which states that measurements of the Milky Way's gravitational field, including its dark matter, redraws the sun's frontier. That theory was put forward by Jim Green, former NASA chief scientist and past director of the space agency's Planetary Science Division, along with Ed Belbruno, a professor of mathematics at Yeshiva University and a senior research associate at Princeton University. The solar system's gravitational frontier extends to nearly 3.8 light-years from the sun , they contend, roughly 241,000 astronomical units (AU), a distance that brings the "edge" of the solar system to within the same scale as the separation between neighboring stars. The edge of our solar system may be defined not by a sharp boundary, but by a "complex dance among forces, energies and trajectories," they write. Green and Belbruno recently made their case in the August 2026 issue of the magazine ROOM - the Space Journal of Asgardia. Slow moving objects Moreover, this theory claims that the gravitationally stable Solar Lagrange points L1 and L2 could form a type of "portal" that could funnel future interstellar visitors such as the recent comet 3I/ATLAS into the solar system, perhaps allowing scientists to capture them for future study. "Discovering the solar-galactic center L1 location is important since slow moving objects that enter this region can be captured by our sun and become part of our solar system," Green told Space.com. "Who knows if there may be a large captured rogue planet on its way into the solar system right now," he said. Green said there's a need to look at these newly calculated L1 and L2 locations to see what could be found. He is now in discussion about making such observations with the New Horizons spacecraft team that explored Pluto in 2015 and is now operating in the outer heliosphere. "Even accumulated dust in this region could verify many of the calculations we have made including the extent of the dark matter in our galaxy," said Green. A diagram showing the Lagrange points L1 though L5. (Image credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Scientific Visualization Studio) Ballistic capture "It's a really nice and significant result," Belbruno told Space.com. The ROOM article, written for a popular audience, draws from his August 2025 keynote lecture at the Niels Bohr Institute. Much of the theory also stems from Belbruno's work on permanent capture into the solar system and weak stability boundaries published in 2024 in the journal Celestial Mechanics and Dynamical Astronomy. Belbruno authored the book Fly Me to the Moon: An Insider's Guide to the New Science of Space Travel (Princeton University Press, Princeton, 2007). In that work, he spells out how to harness low-fuel space travel he likens to "surfing the gravitational field." "This new work represents a new application of weak stability boundary theory, first applied in 1987 to find new routes to Earth's moon, using ballistic capture for spacecraft," Belbruno said. "Now, its application is substantially extended to ballistic capture into our solar system from interstellar space and in estimating the size of our solar system," he said. Green and Belbruno point out that the very recent discovery of interstellar objects — such as interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS in 2025 — passing through our solar system on hyperbolic trajectories "has opened an entirely new window onto the material and processes shaping planetary systems across the galaxy." Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS as seen by the Hubble Space Telescope in August 2025 as it passed through our solar system. (Image credit: NASA/ESA/David Jewitt (UCLA)/ Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI)) Mastery of gravity The article in ROOM adds some impactful ideas regarding potential distant alien civilizations. "Interstellar travel requires a mastery of gravity, which an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might use to tour the galaxy, using portals created at Lagrange points for leverage, Green and Belbruno write. "Remaining at these locations, they could observe the life within a stellar system with essentially no energy expenditure," the researchers add, "so perhaps we should be looking for large space stations at stellar L1 and L2 locations as a techno-signature of advanced intelligent life?"

item.title: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors
item.description: PC; Origame Digital This odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appears A Nazi kneels down on frozen snow, staring at an endless Antarctic horizon. Another holds a gun to his head, ready to end his own life. I direct a small waddling penguin up to them, trying to imagine what it could be thinking. Dismay, perhaps. Likely bewilderment. But then a faint smile seems to break out across its beaky face, as if amused by these silly humans and their misguided belief that they could ever best this howling, harsh landscape. For most games, the idea of playing as a penguin observing Nazis losing the plot near the south pole would be weird enough. But Penguin Colony, developed by Origame Digital, pushes further. This is an audacious, frequently brilliant retelling of HP Lovecraft’s 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness, in which eldritch horrors are just as common as Nazis. Further weirdness abounds: the many collectibles scattered about this place are not shiny gold objects à la Super Mario or Sonic. Rather, they are words. So tottering about as a semiaquatic bird, you have a unique mission: collect human language. Continue reading...

item.title: Do Your Social Media Posts Truly Reflect Who You Are?
item.description: Perhaps one of the most disingenuous things we say to ourselves is that our social media posts do not reflect our true personality . In people’s bios, you see “I’m here for fun, my tweets are not me”, and it sounds really cool. After all, aren’t we all meant to simply have fun on IG or TikTok and keep it moving? Or enjoy a debate with a random stranger and move on? What makes the things we say and how we say them a big deal? However, arguments have shown that our social media presence can present an accurate depiction of who we are in real life, even if we do not want it to be so. Dr Margeret Hall and Dr Simon Caton once tried to find out how much of people’s personalities can be revealed through their social media presence. “We were looking for the ‘Big 5’: openness to experience, conscientiousness, extraversion, agreeableness and neuroticism. We found that we could predict where a person fell on the scale for each trait with a high level of accuracy. Posts about TV programmes were particularly revealing.” After studying about 500 people on Facebook, they concluded that someone, perhaps a potential employer, can possibly observe your personality through your social media pages. Perhaps it would be rash to swiftly form an opinion on who a person is through their social media posts. One could agree that social media is not real life, and we sometimes decide how we want people to perceive us. People can create fake personalities for themselves online to appease other people. Others may use social media to satisfy their alter egos or embody a part of themselves they wish they could be in the real world – like an introvert being quite extroverted online. Or a shy person being super friendly and popular on a social app. But how much of ourselves can we possibly tuck away before it all comes flooding out, and for how long too? What happens when people observe a certain pattern in the way you write, talk and act over the years? Especially when they are detrimental to a certain social group. The world of social media often witnesses people apologising for something they said or did years ago, insisting that those posts, videos or tweets do not reflect their true personality and were borne of naivety or comedy. For instance, a certain user wrote a certain thread, apologising for times he has hurt women on Twitter (now X) through his tweets. He insisted he was young and foolish and the tweets do not reflect his current personality. But between 2013 and 2023, his tweets were consistent – they were what he called jokes about sexually assaulting women. For 10 years, he had consistently tweeted about abusing women, insisting that if he was in a certain power dynamic where he had to relate with female workers or students, he was going to take advantage of them sexually. But his apology had words like “young and foolish” and “no longer reflects my personality”, but if for 10 years, people identified you as an abuser through your tweets, isn’t that simply who you

We found that we could predict where a person fell on the scale for each trait with a high level of accuracy. Posts about TV programmes were particularly revealing.” After studying about 500 people on Facebook, they concluded that someone, perhaps a potential employer, can possibly observe your personality through your social media pages. Perhaps it would be rash to swiftly form an opinion on who a person is through their social media posts. One could agree that social media is not real life, and we sometimes decide how we want people to perceive us. People can create fake personalities for themselves online to appease other people. Others may use social media to satisfy their alter egos or embody a part of themselves they wish they could be in the real world – like an introvert being quite extroverted online. Or a shy person being super friendly and popular on a social app. But how much of ourselves can we possibly tuck away before it all comes flooding out, and for how long too? What happens when people observe a certain pattern in the way you write, talk and act over the years? Especially when they are detrimental to a certain social group. The world of social media often witnesses people apologising for something they said or did years ago, insisting that those posts, videos or tweets do not reflect their true personality and were borne of naivety or comedy. For instance, a certain user wrote a certain thread, apologising for times he has hurt women on Twitter (now X) through his tweets. He insisted he was young and foolish and the tweets do not reflect his current personality. But between 2013 and 2023, his tweets were consistent – they were what he called jokes about sexually assaulting women. For 10 years, he had consistently tweeted about abusing women, insisting that if he was in a certain power dynamic where he had to relate with female workers or students, he was going to take advantage of them sexually. But his apology had words like “young and foolish” and “no longer reflects my personality”, but if for 10 years, people identified you as an abuser through your tweets, isn’t that simply who you are? So, does the way one uses social media portray who they are, and would it not be out of place for people to make assumptions about you based on what you tweet? When I meet someone new offline or online, I check out their tweets to get a glimpse of their thought processes. Social media provides a faux sense of anonymity and security that gets people careless and prone to baring their innermost thoughts with little care for how far their posts can travel. On other social apps, it could take more effort – make a video, or post a picture with captions – but on Twitter, it is seamless; you simply need to talk without giving it too much thought or effort. So if your tweets are filled with misogyny, insults, abuse, and so much anger and bile for other users, isn’t it a glimpse of who you are? What makes you think people would want someone like you in their spaces, online or offline? Why would they wait to meet you physically to truly get to know you? Wouldn’t they be justified in keeping you at bay? One can keep saying that our tweets or social media posts are not who we are, or we can be honest and use them as mirrors, holding them up high to see our reflections. *** Feature Image by Ketut Subiyanto for Pexels The post Do Your Social Media Posts Truly Reflect Who You Are? appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. item.title: From Morning Rush to Nights Out: How Lagos Moves With Every Mood
item.description: In Lagos, the day can take you in a hundred different directions. There’s the morning rush to beat traffic, the lunch date squeezed into a busy afternoon, the quick stop to pick something up, and the dinner plans that turn into a night out. Every day comes with its own agenda, and how you get around often depends on what’s on it. Bolt’s mobility data offers a glimpse into how these everyday routines shape the way Lagos moves. The Everyday Lagos Hustle For many Lagosians, getting to work, making an appointment or heading across town is simply part of the daily routine. It’s no surprise that Bolt’s Standard category accounts for approximately 86% of rides in Lagos on both weekdays and weekends. Whether it’s the morning commute or a weekend errand, everyday journeys remain at the heart of city life. But not every trip is just about getting from A to B. For a business meeting, a special outing or simply a preference for a more comfortable experience, Comfort offers another option. It accounts for roughly 12% of rides in Lagos, consistently across weekdays and weekends, showing that a more premium ride isn’t reserved for special occasions. Quick Errands and Afternoon Plans Sometimes, the destination is just around the corner. In selected areas such as Somolu, Gbagada and Ikeja, Bolt’s three-wheeler category caters to shorter trips, averaging just 2.8 kilometres compared with around 12 kilometres for Standard and Comfort rides. And then there are the things that need to get somewhere, even when you can’t make the trip yourself. Bolt Send helps people move packages around the city, with demand following the rhythm of the working week. Orders peak between 1 p.m. and 3 p.m., when work, errands and last-minute requests often overlap, while Sundays see around half the order volume of a typical weekday. When Lagos Comes Alive After Dark As evening sets in, the city makes room for dinner dates, birthdays, concerts and spontaneous plans with friends. Bolt’s data shows that Comfort accounts for a higher share of orders after 8 p.m. than during the early evening, suggesting that some riders lean towards a more premium experience as the night unfolds. For plans beyond the city, Bolt’s Intercity option connects Lagos with Ibadan, while airport trips in Lagos average around 17 kilometres, whether the journey involves catching a flight or welcoming someone home. Every Day, a Different Plan The beauty of Lagos is that no two days have to look alike. One day might be about work and errands; the next could be brunch, shopping, a concert or a spontaneous night out. The data reflects these different rhythms, from everyday commutes and short neighbourhood trips to afternoon deliveries and evening outings. Ultimately, how people move around the city is shaped by the lives they lead and the plans they make. Any Season, Any Reason. Because in Lagos, every day comes with a different plan. Need a little inspiration for your next Lagos outing? Watch This. Sponsored Content The

item.title: Blaqbonez Releases New Album “NOMADINHO: 4TH PRIME”
item.description: Blaqbonez Releases New Album, Nomadinho: 4th Prime Nigerian rapper Blaqbonez has released his fifth studio album, NOMADINHO: 4TH PRIME, a 15-track project featuring Asake , Victony , Ruger , TML Vibez , Igwe Aka and Monochrome . Released Friday, October 16, 2026, through Chocolate City Music, the album follows his 2025 project, No Excuses, and its April 2026 deluxe edition. The album includes Blaqbonez’s previously released singles “BIG PERFORMER,” “IKEBE 3000” and “CHANEL,” his two collaborations with Asake. “CHANEL” particularly marked a major career milestone for the rapper, earning him his first No. 1 on the Official Nigeria Top 100, while “IKEBE 3000” continued the pair’s run of collaborations. Blaqbonez Releases New Album, Nomadinho: 4th Prime The project opens with “I LOVE THIS,” featuring Igwe Aka, before moving into tracks such as “CA$H EVERYDAY,” “BIG PERFORMER” and “MAZZA.” Other songs include “YAHOOZE,” featuring Victony; “FYP,” featuring Monochrome; “JUSTINA,” featuring Ruger; and “FINESSE YOU,” featuring TML Vibez. With NOMADINHO: 4TH PRIME, Blaqbonez continues to explore the intersection of Nigerian hip-hop and Afrobeats, bringing together established collaborators and emerging voices across the 15-track project. Listen to the album here . The post Blaqbonez Releases New Album “NOMADINHO: 4TH PRIME” appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Fireboy DML’s Fifth Studio Album “ZUKO!” Is Here | Listen!
item.description: Fireboy DML announces the release of his first studio album, ZUKO! Photo credit: Fireboy DML/Instagram . Fireboy DML has arrived, again! The Nigerian singer is known as one of the most talented Afrobeats artists in recent times. To date, he remains the only Nigerian artist with a debut album without any features. But since his debut album, Laughter, Tears and Goosebumps in 2019, Fireboy DML, like any creative, has evolved into different personas and identities. He has released his fifth studio album, ZUKO!, a 13-track project featuring Nigerian artistes Lojay and Judah Earl , Jamaican dancehall star Masicka , and South African acts JAZZWRLD and Thukuthela , and it is another invention of Fireboy DML. Released through YBNL Nation and EMPIRE, ZUKO! arrives two years after his fourth studio project, Adedamola , which was released in 2024. The album opens with “Dear Father,” featuring Judah Earl, followed by “By Fire!” and “CLAAT!”, featuring Masicka. Other tracks include “GODDESS,” featuring Lojay, and “IMALI,” featuring JAZZWRLD and Thukuthela. The remaining songs are “C’EST LA VIE,” “ONE MAN REGIMENT,” “KILOWI,” “ONAZO!,” “S.L.U.T (SEX LOVE UNDERSTANDING TRUST),” “LIGHT OF DAWN,” “MIMI NAWE” and “FIGHTING.” Ahead of the album’s release, Fireboy shared THE RED COUCH SESSION: ZUKO! on YouTube, giving fans a look into the project’s rollout, and an explanation of the theme and title behind the album. ZUKO! follows Fireboy’s previous albums Laughter, Tears and Goosebumps (2019), APOLLO (2020), Playboy (2022) and Adedamola (2024), adding another chapter to his evolving sound and catalogue. Listen to the album here . The post Fireboy DML’s Fifth Studio Album “ZUKO!” Is Here | Listen! appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Astronomers discover the 1st ever green star, a cosmic zombie just in time for Halloween
item.description: null How awesome would it be if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween? It turns out that scientists have discovered that our star may indeed go green, but only billions of years from now after its death — and only if it then starts eating planets like a cosmic zombie. That's possible because scientists have discovered that white dwarfs, the type of stellar remnants sun-sized stars leave behind when they die, can actually take on a range of colors including green if they snack on their rocky planets like cosmic cannibals. For stellar scientists, the colors of stars have always been indicative of their temperatures. Cool stars look orange, while stars like the sun look white , and the hottest stars glow pale blue. This is akin to a blacksmith's iron glowing red, then orange, then white-hot as it heats up. Researchers have always assumed that white dwarfs follow the same rule. However, new research suggests that these stellar corpses could glow in a range of colors including green, pink, cyan, yellow, and purple. That means the universe is far more colorful than we suspected. "Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like 'perfect radiators,' so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs," team leader Mark Hollands of the University of Warwick said in a statement sent to Space.com. "It turns out these incredibly dense stars caaaaan produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me." How white dwarfs break stellar color rules White dwarfs get their name because when they were discovered, they appeared surprisingly hot and glowed white or pale blue. However, this new research suggests that this slightly bland and uniform appearance is because no white dwarf is close enough for Earthbound astronomers to see their true colors. The key to the rainbow-like array of colors this team suggests white dwarfs could possess is their density. White dwarfs form when stars with a mass roughly that of the sun run out of fuel and can no longer support themselves against their own gravity, causing their cores to collapse. As a result, the matter that makes up white dwarfs is around the density of water, millions of times denser than the sun's surface, the photosphere. In these conditions, elements like carbon, calcium, and sodium can interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colors than they would at lower densities. That shifts the colors of white dwarfs away from the white/light blue seen for a perfect radiator of heat. Colour-accurate simulated images of white dwarfs. item.content:encoded: null How awesome would it be if the sun could take on a spooky green glow for Halloween? It turns out that scientists have discovered that our star may indeed go green, but only billions of years from now after its death — and only if it then starts eating planets like a cosmic zombie. That's possible because scientists have discovered that white dwarfs, the type of stellar remnants sun-sized stars leave behind when they die, can actually take on a range of colors including green if they snack on their rocky planets like cosmic cannibals. For stellar scientists, the colors of stars have always been indicative of their temperatures. Cool stars look orange, while stars like the sun look white , and the hottest stars glow pale blue. This is akin to a blacksmith's iron glowing red, then orange, then white-hot as it heats up. Researchers have always assumed that white dwarfs follow the same rule. However, new research suggests that these stellar corpses could glow in a range of colors including green, pink, cyan, yellow, and purple. That means the universe is far more colorful than we suspected. "Most stars, including most white dwarfs, behave like 'perfect radiators,' so their color is set almost entirely by temperature. But nobody had really looked into what else might be possible for white dwarfs," team leader Mark Hollands of the University of Warwick said in a statement sent to Space.com. "It turns out these incredibly dense stars caaaaan produce colors nobody expected, and some of them genuinely surprised me." How white dwarfs break stellar color rules White dwarfs get their name because when they were discovered, they appeared surprisingly hot and glowed white or pale blue. However, this new research suggests that this slightly bland and uniform appearance is because no white dwarf is close enough for Earthbound astronomers to see their true colors. The key to the rainbow-like array of colors this team suggests white dwarfs could possess is their density. White dwarfs form when stars with a mass roughly that of the sun run out of fuel and can no longer support themselves against their own gravity, causing their cores to collapse. As a result, the matter that makes up white dwarfs is around the density of water, millions of times denser than the sun's surface, the photosphere. In these conditions, elements like carbon, calcium, and sodium can interact with the surrounding dense helium plasma and absorb light across a wider range of colors than they would at lower densities. That shifts the colors of white dwarfs away from the white/light blue seen for a perfect radiator of heat. Colour-accurate simulated images of white dwarfs. (Image credit: Mark Hollands/University of Warwick) The researchers found that the colors of white dwarfs would fit into distinct groups tied to the individual chemical makeup of the stellar remnant's atmosphere. White dwarfs abundant in carbon should be pink or purple, while those that have been enriched with debris from consumed asteroids and comets, and the remains of old planetary systems, would take a more yellow hue. Cooler white dwarfs with mixed hydrogen and helium atmospheres often would glow cyan or pale blue, caused as hydrogen molecules collide with helium atoms in their dense atmospheres. One of the most striking examples of white dwarf coloration, however, would arise when one of these living dead stars starts feeding on the planets around it like a horror movie zombie. Zombie white dwarfs go green The researchers found that some dead star white dwarfs can go a little green around the gills after snacking on orbiting planets. An example of this is WD J1330+6435, a cool white dwarf located around 326 light-years away, which has been accreting rocky material from a planetary companion. This has enriched its atmosphere with calcium, lithium, and sodium, and the team's model suggests this would have led WD J1330+6435 to adopt a green hue. But unlike the green-tinged zombies of George Romero's classic Dawn of the Dead, there are no hordes of these green-faced cosmic zombies ... yet. The researchers think that no other star, living or dead, has ever been credibly reported as green. That makes WD J1330+6435 the first known genuinely green star. An illustration of a green star (Image credit: Robert Lea (created with Canva)) "The traces of sodium in the atmosphere of this white dwarf absorb the orange part of the spectrum, leaving behind a ghostly green glow," Hollands said. "Imagine standing on a planet and looking up at a green star. It feels like something out of science fiction ." Scientists see red The team didn't just discover that a known white dwarf is the first-ever green star; they also discovered what could be the reddest star ever in the form of the white dwarf WD J1011+2845. Located just 48 light-years from Earth, this white dwarf has a deep convection zone that carries carbon from its core to its surface. These carbon molecules distort light from the white dwarf, causing a deep salmon-pink glow unlike anything seen in any other star. Enriched from below: The cool white dwarf WDJ0902+2010 has a deep convection zone within its helium dominated outer envelope. (Image credit: Mark A. Garlick/University of Warwick) Despite this rainbow of white dwarfs, the team theorizes that white is still the most common color for these stellar corpses. Only five of the 151 white dwarfs within around 65 light-years of Earth have extraordinary coloring. Extrapolating this to the total population of white dwarfs, the team estimates that only one in 30 of these dead stars has an unusual color. "One in thirty might not sound like a huge fraction, but across the entire population of white dwarfs in the universe, that is still a lot of oddly colored stars out there," Boris Gänsicke, Department of Physics, University of Warwick, said. "Yet if we take the median across a representative population of white dwarfs, we found that the average white dwarf really is white." The team's research was published on Thursday (Oct. 14) in the journal RAS Techniques and Instruments.

item.title: On this day in space! Oct. 15, 1997: NASA launches Cassini-Hugyens probe on 7-year voyage to Saturn
item.description: null On Oct. 15, 1997, NASA launched the Cassini spacecraft on a mission to explore Saturn and its moons. It lifted off aboard a Titan 4B rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. It took almost seven years for the Cassini spacecraft to reach Saturn , with the spacecraft entering orbit around the ringed planet in 2004. Another smaller spacecraft called Huygens hitched a ride with Cassini, and it landed on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005. Cassini spent 13 years studying the Saturn system up close, and the mission lasted about 20 years before coming to an epic grand finale on Sept. 15, 2017 . Running low on fuel, NASA chose to steer Cassini straight into Saturn's atmosphere, where the spacecraft was destroyed . NASA's Cassini spacecraft lifts off on Oct. 15, 1997, atop a Titan IVB rocket. (Image credit: NASA) Why it mattered NASA's Cassini mission to Saturn (which carried the European Space Agency's Huygens lander to Titan) was a flagship planetary mission like no other ever when it first launched toward the ringed planet. The $3.26 billion Cassini spacecraft became the first probe ever to orbit Saturn when it arrived in 2004. It revealed Saturn's rings as active and dynamic structures, as intricate and complex as they are beautiful to observe. And it delivered Huygens to Titan, then followed up with a series of Titan flybys that revealed the cloudy moon could have liquid hydrocarbon rain, rivers, lakes and seas. Perhaps the most exciting discoveries were the most surprising. Cassini discovered a strange hexagon-shaped jetstream encircling Saturn's north pole and revealed massive hurricane-like vortexes over both of the planet's poles. In 2010, Cassini watched as a giant storm formed in Saturn's northern hemisphere, then grew to encircle the entire planet through 2011. The spacecraft also discovered icy plumes of water erupting from Saturn's moon Enceladus , revealing new clues into that moon's subsurface ocean of liquid water, complete with hydrothermal events like those found in Earth's oceans. This artist's illustration shows Cassini making one of its final five dives through Saturn's upper atmosphere in August and September 2017. (Image credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech ) It was to protect Enceladus, Titan and other Saturn moons that NASA ultimated sent Cassini into a death dive into Saturn at the end of its mission. The space agency wanted to prevent any chance of contamination at those pristine moons. "NASA’s Cassini spacecraft and ESA’s Huygens probe expanded our understanding of the kinds of worlds where life might exist and eight more reasons the mission changed the course of planetary exploration," NASA said in an overview .
